Differentiable Exact Learning

Hristo Papazov ††thanks: Corresponding author: hristo.papazov@epfl.ch    Francesco D’Angelo    Nicolas Flammarion Affiliation: Department of Computer Science, EPFL
Abstract

We introduce a framework for differentiable exact learning that couples an unbounded external environment to a state-tracking neural controller, which we train on policy-trajectory observations (PTOs): expert behavior traces that expose observations and actions while hiding internal states. In addition to the learning framework, we introduce Differentiable Finite-State Transducers (DFSTs) which use multilinear updates, support log-parallel training, and emulate arbitrary finite-state controllers, yielding computational universality through environmental interaction. From tiny training datasets, compact DFSTs achieve extreme length generalization on arithmetic and universal-simulation tasks. We replicate the success of DFSTs on RNNs and GRUs, thereby supporting a broader learning recipe: State-Tracking Controller + Unbounded External Environment + PTOs = Extreme Length Generalization. Beyond length generalization, our metric-extraction protocol recovers interpretable discrete controllers from trained DFSTs, which we prove equivalent to the target arithmetic and universal-simulation algorithms. Furthermore, for our Softmax DFST models, simply taking argmax\argmax over the transition probabilities yields discrete controllers which provably exactly perform universal Turing-machine simulation and binary arithmetic. Proving exact learning for the neural controllers requires assumptions, which we empirically support. We make our code, training recipes, model weights, and proof checkers publicly available.

1 Introduction

For decades, researchers have sought to make neural networks learn algorithmic procedures from data, arguing that genuine machine intelligence requires exact recovery of underlying rules rather than matching surface-level statistics (Solomonoff and others, 2006; György et al., 2025).

Yet arithmetic, the canonical testbed for algorithmic learning, continues to expose a persistent gap. Transformers and RNNs trained on input-output data generalize only marginally to longer inputs (Delétang et al., 2022). Even an extensive arsenal of scratchpad protocols, positional-encoding schemes, and input-formatting tricks brings Transformer length generalization11 1 Defined in the referenced papers as achieving above 95% exact-match accuracy (EMA). to 22–7×7\times the training operand length, with exact-match accuracy swiftly decaying as inputs lengthen (Hou et al., 2025; Y. Zhou et al., 2024; Cho et al., 2024a). The Neural GPU (Kaiser and Sutskever, 2015) stands out by reaching 100×100\times length generalization on random binary arithmetic instances, although later diagnostics expose long-carry and symmetric-input failures (Price et al., 2016) (see Table 1). Such finite-test success leaves exactness on arbitrarily long inputs unresolved.

A relevant exception comes from the recursive Neural Programmer-Interpreter (NPI) (Reed and De Freitas, 2015; Cai et al., 2017), which provably recovers decimal addition and several sorting algorithms. However, the training uses a stronger form of supervision through recursive call/return annotations that goes beyond merely observing expert actions in an external environment.

In contrast, real learners routinely succeed under exactly this restriction. Indeed, children acquire complex procedural skills by observing adults perform goal-directed actions, with no access to the adults’ internal neural processes. From such behavior traces alone, infants infer the underlying procedural structure and reproduce the target behavior through practice (Meltzoff and Moore, 1995).

Motivated by the success of natural learners, this paper entertains the idea of gradient-based exact algorithmic learning from behavior observations and provides a simple recipe for achieving extreme length generalization with compact controllers trained from scratch on small datasets (see Figure 1). To our knowledge, this work provides the first differentiable exact recovery of a fixed universal interpreter with correctness proofs covering arbitrary simulations of Turing machines with unbounded input lengths and unbounded execution horizons. We similarly achieve exact differentiable recovery on addition and multiplication tasks. Our training withholds expert control states and the learned interpreter requires no retraining when exchanging input programs. We just need two ingredients: sufficiently informative observations and a sufficiently expressive learner.

Sufficiently Informative Observations. The choice of training data determines the possibility of exact learning. Gold (1967) proved that no algorithm can identify the class of recursive functions in the limit from input–output examples alone (Gold, 1967, Theorem I.5). Moreover, the impossibility persists in the active-learning setting (Gold, 1967, Theorem I.3). Hence, supervised learning from (z,f⁡(z))(z,f(z)) pairs and reinforcement learning rewarded only for correct output without a helpful curriculum cannot identify every recursive function in general. To navigate between this general identification barrier and the additional (strong and unrealistic) program-structure supervision of NPIs, we adopt policy-trajectory observations (PTOs) as our training signal. PTOs record how the environment evolves under the expert’s policy without exposing the expert’s internal state transitions.22 2 Recovering an algorithm with PTOs mirrors more realistic learning-from-demonstration settings (Argall et al., 2009). This middle ground carries two advantages: (i) PTOs avoid Gold’s impossibility barrier (Papazov and Flammarion, 2025, Theorem 16); (ii) PTOs admit a natural interpretation as behavior observations – the learner only observes how the world changes under the expert’s actions.

Sufficiently Expressive Learner. Since we target exact learning of arbitrary algorithms, the learner must belong to a Turing-complete model class. Prior work establishes Turing-completeness for Transformers and RNNs through assumptions that preclude effective optimization: unbounded arithmetic precision (Siegelmann and Sontag, 1992; Pérez et al., 2019), unbounded context windows (Dehghani et al., 2018; Bhattamishra et al., 2020; Merrill and Sabharwal, 2023a), or non-differentiable environmental interaction (Chung and Siegelmann, 2021; Schuurmans et al., 2024). We propose a simpler workaround that preserves finite precision and fixed-size contexts, allowing for effective gradient-based optimization. The key idea couples a state-tracking33 3 We define state-tracking as capable of simulating arbitrary finite-state automata given sufficient model capacity. controller – such as an RNN, LSTM, or GRU – to a dynamically resizing external environment in which the controller can move, read, and write. Because the environment grows as needed, computation no longer bottlenecks on the controller’s fixed internal memory. Zaremba and Sutskever (2015) explored a related architecture pairing an LSTM controller with external tapes, but trained via reinforcement learning on input–output rewards alone, which Gold’s theorem renders insufficient for exact learning in general. We hope to revive and strengthen this architectural idea through the richer PTO supervision.

Thus, our learning recipe distills into a simple equation:

State-Tracking Controller + Unbounded External Environment + PTOs = Extreme Length Generalization.

In fact, we go a step further and introduce a simple extraction procedure, which recovers discrete controllers from our trained neural models. We prove that the extracted controllers exactly follow the target behavior and hence certify the following method for differentiable exact learning of algorithms:

Main Contributions.

  1. 1.

    A Conceptual Framework for Differentiable Exact Learning. We revive the idea of achieving Turing-complete differentiable computation through a state-tracking neural controller coupled to an unbounded external environment. Training on a small number of PTOs yields extreme length generalization. Subsequent extraction establishes exact learning for the recovered discrete controllers across the studied tasks and for the neural controllers subject to stability assumptions.

  2. 2.

    Differentiable Finite-State Transducers (DFSTs). We introduce a (i) minimalist, (ii) multilinear, (iii) differentiable, (iv) state-tracking, and (v) parallelizable model family whose members serve as controllers in our experiments. DFSTs use no nonlinear activations, admit log-parallel training via prefix scans (Blelloch, 1990), and offer a transparent structure for studying the loss landscape of algorithmic learning and the useful implicit bias of gradient descent.

  3. 3.

    Extreme Generalization from Small PTO Datasets. We train on small PTO datasets (25 traces for add2, 100 for mult2, 250 for add10, and 10000 for mult10) and reach robust testing caps of 5000 digits for addition and 1000 digits for multiplication. The training operands contain at most 3 and 5 digits, respectively. We replicate the extreme length generalization on binary arithmetic using RNN and GRU controllers thereby supporting our generalization recipe.

  4. 4.

    Exact Learning of a Universal Controller. A 4335-parameter DFST trained from scratch on just 75 PTOs from 5 program simulations over inputs of at most 5 symbols reaches the 500-symbol evaluation cap across 10 tasks, including 5 held-out programs. From trained DFST models, our extraction procedures recover controllers provably equivalent to the expert universal interpreter and capable of simulating arbitrary programs on any input lengths and execution horizons.

  5. 5.

    Extraction and Verification of Exact Learning. A lightweight extraction procedure applied to trained DFSTs recovers compact FSTs. Eight proofs establish exact expert-policy equivalence across binary and decimal arithmetic and universal simulation. Additional empirically verified assumptions prove the equivalence of the trained neural controllers to the experts.

Remark. An earlier workshop version introduced DFSTs and reported considerable arithmetic length generalization (Papazov et al., 2025). The present work simplifies training; pushes length generalization to the extreme; and adds learned universal simulation, Softmax DFSTs, recurrent-controller comparisons, and exact-equivalence certificates for extracted controllers.

Paper Organization. Section 2 formalizes PTO-learning, DFSTs, and the studied algorithmic tasks. Section 3 expands on our arithmetic and universal experiments, with a short passage on the implicit bias of gradient descent. Section 4 explains FST extraction and verification of correctness. We refer the reader to Appendix A for a thorough discussion of related work.

2 Preliminaries

As discussed in the introduction, our recipe for exact learning couples a state-tracking controller to an unbounded external environment.

2.1 Policy-Trajectory Observations

We model the external environment as a symbolic grid.

Definition 2.1 (Symbolic Grid).

Given a finite alphabet Σ\Sigma containing the empty symbol λ{\lambda}, a grid configuration w:ℤ2→Σw:{\mathbb{Z}}^{2}\to\Sigma assigns a symbol w⁡(p)∈Σw(p)\in\Sigma to each cell p∈ℤ2p\in{\mathbb{Z}}^{2} such that only finitely many cells differ from λ{\lambda}. The symbolic grid 𝒢=𝒢⁡(ℤ2,Σ)\mathcal{G}=\mathcal{G}({\mathbb{Z}}^{2},\Sigma) denotes the set of all such configurations.

The finiteness requirement captures the idea that the environment grows as needed but never stores an infinite amount of information at any point in time. We now formalize the agents that inhabit the grid.

Definition 2.2 (Grid Agent).

A grid agent over the symbolic grid 𝒢⁡(ℤ2,Σ)\mathcal{G}({\mathbb{Z}}^{2},\Sigma) stands for a finite-state transducer T=(Q,Σ,Γ,δ,γ,q0,qf)T=(Q,\Sigma,\Gamma,{\delta},{\gamma},q_{0},q_{f}), where QQ denotes a finite set of states, Σ\Sigma serves as both the read alphabet and the write alphabet, Γ=Σ×ℳ\Gamma=\Sigma\times{\mathcal{M}} with ℳ={L,R,U,D,S}{\mathcal{M}}=\{\texttt{L},\texttt{R},\texttt{U},\texttt{D},\texttt{S}\} forms the output alphabet pairing a grid symbol with a motion direction, δ:Q×Σ→Q{\delta}:Q\times\Sigma\to Q specifies the state-transition function, γ:Q×Σ→Γ{\gamma}:Q\times\Sigma\to\Gamma specifies the output function, q0∈Qq_{0}\in Q denotes the initial state, and qf∈Qq_{f}\in Q denotes the halting state. The agent always starts at p0=(0,0)p_{0}=(0,0).

The agent occupies a single cell pt∈ℤ2p_{t}\in{\mathbb{Z}}^{2} at each time step tt, reads the symbol xt+1=wt​(pt)x_{t+1}=w_{t}(p_{t}), produces an output γ⁡(qt,xt+1)=(st+1,mt+1){\gamma}(q_{t},x_{t+1})=(s_{t+1},m_{t+1}) that writes st+1s_{t+1} at position ptp_{t} and shifts the agent’s position by mt+1m_{t+1}, and transitions to state δ⁡(qt,xt+1){\delta}(q_{t},x_{t+1}). We adopt the convention that every transition containing the stop motion S leads to the halting state qfq_{f}, and all transitions from qfq_{f} satisfy δ⁡(qf,x)=qf{\delta}(q_{f},x)=q_{f} and γ⁡(qf,x)=(x,S){\gamma}(q_{f},x)=(x,\texttt{S}) for every x∈Σx\in\Sigma, rendering qfq_{f} a dead state that leaves the grid unchanged.

Note that a grid agent perceives only one cell at a time. Future work could explore richer perception mechanisms encoding the contents of multiple cells and agents interacting with a larger motion vocabulary. Since standard Turing machines arise as a special case of grid agents restricted to a single row, the class 𝒜{\mathcal{A}} of all grid agents achieves computational universality when interacting with 𝒢{\mathcal{G}}.

PTOs. At each time step tt, an external learner observing agent TT perceives only the written symbol st∈Σs_{t}\in\Sigma, the motion mt∈ℳm_{t}\in{\mathcal{M}}, and the observation xtx_{t} that triggered the action. Importantly, the internal state qtq_{t} remains hidden. The resulting sequence (xt,st,mt)t=1T(x_{t},s_{t},m_{t})_{t=1}^{T} constitutes a policy-trajectory observation (PTO), matching the formalism of Papazov and Flammarion (2025). Crucially, Papazov and Flammarion (2025, Theorem 16) proved that PTOs enable exact identification of any computable function in the limit – a guarantee unachievable through input–output supervision alone (Gold, 1967).

Hardness. Each algorithmic task 𝒫\mathcal{P} comes with a set of valid inputs S𝒫⊆Σ⋆S_{\mathcal{P}}\subseteq{\Sigma^{\star}}. Because the motion token outputted at each step constrains the next observation, S𝒫S_{\mathcal{P}} may never cover all reachable transducer transitions, thereby making the learning problem fundamentally hard. Papazov and Flammarion (2025, Theorem 17) proved that no polynomial-mass characteristic set exists for this restricted-input regime, ruling out any algorithm that learns the policy of every grid agent from polynomially many polynomially long PTOs (see Section C.3 for details).

2.2 State-Tracking Differentiable Controllers

While Papazov and Flammarion (2025, Theorem 16) showed that a learning-by-enumeration strategy provably identifies any grid agent from PTOs, such an approach takes time and memory exponential in the size of the target expert agent. We instead pursue gradient-based learning by introducing a simple differentiable model that can serve as a grid-agent controller.

Definition 2.3 (DFST).

A Differentiable Finite-State Transducer (DFST) of dimension dd over the symbolic grid 𝒢⁡(ℤ2,Σ){\mathcal{G}}({\mathbb{Z}}^{2},\Sigma) with motion vocabulary ℳ{\mathcal{M}} comprises three trainable weight tensors

A∈ℝ|Σ|×d×d,B∈ℝ|Σ|×|Σ|×d,C∈ℝ|Σ|×|ℳ|×d,A\in{\mathbb{R}}^{|\Sigma|\times d\times d},\qquad B\in{\mathbb{R}}^{|\Sigma|\times|\Sigma|\times d},\qquad C\in{\mathbb{R}}^{|\Sigma|\times|{\mathcal{M}}|\times d},

and a trainable initial hidden state h0∈ℝdh_{0}\in{\mathbb{R}}^{d}. At each time step t≥1t\geq 1, the controller reads the one-hot encoding xt∈ℝ|Σ|x_{t}\in{\mathbb{R}}^{|\Sigma|} of the symbol at the current grid cell wt−1​(pt−1)w_{t-1}(p_{t-1}) and computes

ht=A⁡[xt]​ht−1,s^t=B⁡[xt]​ht−1,m^t=C⁡[xt]​ht−1.h_{t}=A[x_{t}]\,h_{t-1},\qquad\hat{s}_{t}=B[x_{t}]\,h_{t-1},\qquad\hat{m}_{t}=C[x_{t}]\,h_{t-1}.

AA drives the hidden-state recurrence, BB produces scores over symbol tokens, and CC produces scores over motion tokens. At inference time, the controller emits σt=argmax(s^t)∈Σ{\sigma}_{t}=\argmax(\hat{s}_{t})\in\Sigma and μt=argmax(m^t)∈ℳ\mu_{t}=\argmax(\hat{m}_{t})\in{\mathcal{M}}, writing σt{\sigma}_{t} at position pt−1p_{t-1} and moving μt\mu_{t} to ptp_{t} (see Figure 2).

The DFST recurrence and readouts use only input-indexed matrix-vector products, without nonlinear activations. This multilinear structure enables log-parallel training via prefix scans (Blelloch, 1990) and yields a compact parametrization. A dd-dimensional DFST over an alphabet of size k=|Σ|k=|\Sigma| with r=|ℳ|r=|{\mathcal{M}}| motion tokens carries k​d​(k+d+r)+dkd(k+d+r)+d trainable parameters, scaling as O⁡(d2)O(d^{2}).

Definition 2.4 (Softmax DFST).

A Softmax DFST has the same recurrence and readout mechanism as a DFST, with trainable logits ΘA,ΘB,ΘC,θh\Theta^{A},\Theta^{B},\Theta^{C},\theta^{h} parametrizing

P[x]:j=softmax(ΘP[x]:j),P∈{A,B,C},h0=softmax(θh).P[x]_{:j}=\operatorname{softmax}(\Theta^{P}[x]_{:j}),\quad P\in\{A,B,C\},\qquad h_{0}=\operatorname{softmax}(\theta^{h}).

Each column sums to one. Thus, the hidden state remains in the probability simplex and the readouts give distributions over writes and motions. Execution uses the same argmax decoding as a DFST.

This parametrization makes extraction transparent: each column assigns probabilities to successors or actions, and concentration near a simplex vertex suggests a deterministic transition. The recurrence retains the associative matrix scan. Section 4 develops differentiable sharpening and the conditions for faithful extraction.

Despite the simplicity of these architectures, both families support state tracking:

Theorem 2.5 (DFST-Grid Universality).

Any dd-state grid agent admits exact emulation by a dd-dimensional DFST at any finite arithmetic precision, and by a (d+1)(d+1)-dimensional Softmax DFST with finite logits in exact real arithmetic. A dd-dimensional Softmax DFST also suffices under rounded arithmetic whose softmax attains simplex vertices and whose recurrence preserves vertex operations.

Consequently, both the DFST and Softmax DFST families achieve Turing-completeness on the symbolic grid under the respective arithmetic conditions. Appendix B gives the constructive proof and discusses non-uniqueness of DFST parametrizations and the relationship between hidden dimension and expert state count.

More broadly, any sequential model capable of emulating a finite-state transducer can represent the policy of a grid agent and thereby compute any computable function on the grid. This class includes RNNs, LSTMs, and GRUs (Alon et al., 1991; Indyk, 1995; Siegelmann, 1996; Weiss et al., 2018; Merrill, 2019; Svete and Cotterell, 2023) whereas standard Transformers and diagonal SSMs face state-tracking limitations as demonstrated by Merrill and Sabharwal (2023b); Merrill et al. (2024). We focus on DFSTs due to the multilinear structure and simplicity of the model class, which we hope will inspire theoretical analysis of the implicit bias of gradient descent toward generalizing solutions. The DFST, RNN, and GRU experiments in Section 3 support this broader state-tracking perspective.

2.3 Experimental Setup

We study grid agents for binary and decimal arithmetic (add2, add10, mult2, mult10) and a universal grid agent UU that simulates Turing machines over the {λ,0,1}\{\lambda,0,1\} alphabet. Table 2 summarizes expert state counts, alphabets, and runtimes for all implemented grid agents and Turing machines.

Arithmetic Tasks.

Each arithmetic agent receives z=a∘bz=a\circ b, with ∘∈{+,×}\circ\in\{+,\times\}, written horizontally on an otherwise empty grid. The agents execute the schoolbook algorithms for addition and multiplication, halting when only the result remains on the grid.

Data Generation. Each arithmetic PTO dataset includes all R2R^{2} pairs of single-digit operands, then samples distinct pairs with independent uniform operand lengths in 1,…,q1,\ldots,q and digits in 0,…,R−10,\ldots,R-1. Leading zeros remain part of the representation. Ordinary DFST datasets always use: add2: q=3q=3, N=25N=25; add10: q=3q=3, N=250N=250; mult2: q=5q=5, N=100N=100; mult10: q=5q=5, N=10​kN=10\text{k}.

Length-Generalization Metrics. Uniform Length Generalization (ULG) records the operand length returned by a capped search requiring perfect next-action exact-match accuracy on ten random pairs of exactly that length. Robust Length Generalization (RLG) additionally requires perfect accuracy on structured repdigit probes and cannot exceed ULG. Every RLG evaluation tests all R2R^{2} repdigit pairs (am,bm)(a^{m},b^{m}) with a,b∈{0,…,R−1}a,b\in\{0,\ldots,R-1\}. Every timestep must match both the expert write and motion. The Neural GPU motivates this distinction: strong generalization on random binary inputs (Kaiser and Sutskever, 2015) can coexist with failure on repdigit instances (Price et al., 2016). Section D.6 specifies the search, numerical execution modes, and limits of finite testing.

Learning a Universal Interpreter.

The universal grid agent UU uses 15 states and alphabet {0,1,λ,X,Y,Z,𝙻,𝚁,𝚂}\{0,1,{\lambda},X,Y,Z,\mathtt{L},\mathtt{R},\mathtt{S}\}. Given an encoding ⟨M,z⟩\langle M,z\rangle of a Turing machine MM and input z∈{0,1}+z\in{\{0,1\}}^{+}, UU simulates MM on zz, halting with M⁡(z)M(z) in a designated grid region whenever MM halts.

UU uses 3 teleportation runes {X,Y,Z}\{X,Y,Z\} to mark and jump directly between grid locations, shortening simulation trajectories. The grid stores an encoding of the currently simulated Turing machine MM together with the input. From PTOs of the universal expert, a differentiable controller learns how to read and execute this program, without access to the internal states or transition map of UU. The public repository provides model weights and animated executions.

Data Generation and Evaluation. Universal datasets contain N∈{75,150,225}N\in\{75,150,225\} PTOs covering 5 programs, with binary input lengths at most 5. After sampling a random string for each program, the rest of the dataset comes from random program–input pairs. Evaluation covers 10 tasks, including 5 held-out programs and scaling tasks that increase both input length and program size. Appendix F details the rune mechanics, program/input encoding, and training and evaluation tasks.

Controller Training.

For each task, a manually designed expert supplies PTOs. We train controllers via next-action prediction with the MSE loss

12​T​∑t=1T[‖s^t−𝟏st‖22+‖m^t−𝟏mt‖22],\frac{1}{2T}\sum_{t=1}^{T}\left[\|\hat{s}_{t}-\mathbf{1}_{s_{t}}\|_{2}^{2}+\|\hat{m}_{t}-\mathbf{1}_{m_{t}}\|_{2}^{2}\right],

where 𝟏st\mathbf{1}_{s_{t}} and 𝟏mt\mathbf{1}_{m_{t}} denote the one-hot encodings of the expert write and motion at time tt. We train DFST controllers on all tasks, study Softmax DFSTs on binary arithmetic and universal simulation, and compare RNN and GRU controllers on binary arithmetic. Training always uses Adam (Kingma, 2014), batch size 32, and float32 precision.

DFST Training. Unless otherwise specified, DFST hidden dimensions match the expert state counts. We always use a simple deterministic initialization. Transition matrices start at the identity, output matrices at zero, and the trainable initial state at 𝟏d\mathbf{1}_{d}. All ordinary DFSTs runs use an exponential warm-up and cool-down learning-rate scheduler(Sections D.1 and D.2). Section B.3 examines successful learning with smaller and larger hidden dimensions.

Softmax DFST Training. Softmax DFSTs apply the same initialization recipe to the logits before softmax normalization. The sweeps use one, two, or three times the expert state count and vary dataset size. Training uses 100k updates at constant learning rate 0.10.1 (and optional annealing towards approximately one-hot transition probabilities). Section D.4 gives the full training settings.

3 Experimental Results and Discussion

In this section, we discuss length-generalization results solely due to differentiable training.

3.1 Length Generalization on Arithmetic

Figure 3 compares arithmetic generalization before extraction. All DFST and Softmax DFST models train from scratch with the same simple deterministic initialization recipe.

Several DFST runs reach both the ULG and RLG testing caps: 5000 digits per operand for addition and 1000 for multiplication, in binary and decimal radix, after training on operands of at most 3 and 5 digits, respectively. Success varies across training schedules, and additional updates need not improve generalization.

After 100k constant learning-rate updates, many Softmax DFST configurations reach the robust binary-addition and multiplication caps. The Softmax DFST runs hold the advantage of providing interpretable transition probabilities while also supporting extreme generalization. However, Softmax DFST optimization proves more challenging, and we could not fit even small training sets on the decimal tasks. Section D.7 discusses these limitations.

Tens of Millions of Consecutive Correct Actions. Operand length understates the scale of this extrapolation. Adding two 5000-digit all-9 numbers requires 50 070 010 PTO steps; multiplying two 1000-digit all-9 numbers requires 15 012 991. Each step requires the correct write and motion, including the final stopping action. The corresponding binary all-1 probes require exactly the same numbers of steps (Section F.5). Successful decimal DFSTs reproduce the all-9 trajectories, while multiple binary DFST and Softmax DFST configurations reproduce the equally long all-1 trajectories. The binary controllers learn from only 25–75 addition PTOs or 100–300 multiplication PTOs on operands of at most 3 or 5 digits, respectively. Such training supports faithful execution over tens of millions of steps on these structured probes, far beyond the short training traces.

Small-Data Learning and Implicit Bias. These long executions raise a question beyond representational capacity: why does gradient-based training favor rules that continue working so far beyond the training lengths? Matching the training PTOs alone does not force such behavior. We construct spurious binary addition and multiplication controllers that reproduce every expert PTO within the training-length bounds, yet stop prematurely on longer inputs. Thus, even exhaustive supervision over the entire 3 or 5-digit input domains cannot distinguish the expert algorithms from these degenerate alternatives. Furthermore, the spurious controllers need only 14 and 38 states (Sections I.1 and I.2), compared to the 11 and 32 states for the binary arithmetic experts.

The larger Softmax DFSTs in Figure 3 have enough capacity to express these spurious solutions: addition uses dimensions 22 and 33, and multiplication uses 64 and 96 (Section I.3). Nevertheless, five of six configurations in each larger sweep reach the robust testing cap. These successful configurations therefore avoid the constructed spurious rules despite sufficient capacity to represent those rules. Gradient-based optimization with the chosen parametrization and initialization repeatedly favors behavior that survives long execution horizons despite the training set failing to distinguish other spurious targets. These results support the existence of a useful implicit bias towards generalizing rules. Characterizing the source and reliability of this bias remains an open direction.

3.2 Length Generalization on the Universal Task

A 15-dimensional DFST with 4,335 parameters, trained on 75 PTOs from 5 programs on inputs of at most 5 symbols, reaches the 500-symbol cap on all 10 universal-simulation tasks (Figure 4). A 30-dimensional Softmax DFST with 12,720 parameters, trained on 150 PTOs, also reaches every task cap. The longest sampled trajectory requires 15,316,822 consecutive expert-action matches (Table 8).

These evaluations test 3 distinct forms of generalization: longer inputs, transfer to 5 unseen programs, and larger encoded Turing machines. Each controller keeps the same learned weights across all evaluations. Thus, a fixed model can execute novel computations without retraining, simply by changing the input Turing machine.

3.3 Controller Families and Training Dynamics

All six DFST, RNN, and GRU runs reach both binary-task caps (Figure 5). Each controller learns from 25 addition PTOs or 100 multiplication PTOs. These results support the same learning recipe across three distinct controller families: state tracking, unbounded external memory, and PTO supervision.

In Figure 5, the loss curves track fitting of the short training PTOs, while the RLG curves measure generalization to long structured inputs. All later recorded checkpoints retain the caps. Intermediate generalization need not improve monotonically, and low training loss does not certify algorithmic correctness. Section E.3 and Table 5 provide the full comparison and complete training settings.

4 Verification of Exact Learning

Beyond the finite length-generalization tests in Section 3, we extract and verify discrete controllers, then identify conditions for transferring correctness to neural execution (Section 1). Even with discrete controllers, the unbounded grid prevents a general sufficient testing horizon:

Lemma 4.1 (Undecidability of Finite-Horizon Verification).

No algorithm can take descriptions of two grid agents T,MT,M and return a finite input-length bound LL such that agreement of the PTOs T⁡[z]=M⁡[z]T[z]=M[z] for every z∈Σ≤Lz\in\Sigma^{\leq L} implies agreement on all inputs.

Section H.1 proves the claim by reduction from the halting problem. Thus, in general, no algorithm can guarantee that length-generalizing up to a certain cap proves exact learning. To certify exact learning, we will have to consider the specific controller structure. And since finite-precision neural controllers represent prohibitively large FSTs, we first need to extract something manageable.

4.1 Recovering Explicit Controllers

Metric Extraction. We feed random inputs to a trained DFST controller and unroll the hidden-state trajectories from the executions. We connect hidden states within ε{\varepsilon} Euclidean distance and cluster the hidden states into connected components which become the initial discrete states. Each discrete state points to other discrete states through symbol transitions inherited from the hidden states inside the connected component. Thus, we have obtained a non-deterministic FST. We begin to merge the discrete states until either we get a deterministic FST and return, or until we get some inconsistency. In case of inconsistency, we halve ε{\varepsilon} and start anew. For some small enough ε{\varepsilon}, we will obtain a consistent deterministic transition graph. The resulting graph reproduces the collected trajectories, leaving unobserved transitions undefined. Interestingly, we empirically verify that after enough sampled hidden-state trajectories, the extracted graph stabilizes. Note that this type of extraction uses no expert hidden-state labels. See Section G.1 for more details.

Softmax Annealing and Direct Readout. A trained Softmax DFST assigns probabilities to successor states and actions. We continue training with a G⁡(p)=1−‖p‖22G(p)=1-\|p\|_{2}^{2} penalty which sharpens the distributions. Progressively increasing (annealing) the penalty weight concentrates the probabilities into approximately one-hot vectors. Column-wise argmax\argmax then selects deterministic discrete transitions, thereby extracting an FST. Section G.2 gives the full objective and schedule.

Both extraction routes produce candidate discrete controllers. Figure 6 shows empirical graph stability and approximate one-hot probability concentration.

4.2 Proving Target Equivalence for the Recovered Algorithms

We relate extracted states and grid configurations to phases of the expert algorithm. The relation holds initially, and we prove that each permitted transition produces matching actions and preserves the relation. Algorithm-specific invariants show that the phases cover every valid execution. Induction then establishes agreement for arbitrary execution lengths, including simultaneous stopping. Different internal representations and state counts can therefore implement the same algorithm (Section H.3).

Eight Certificates. We provide five metric-extraction and three annealing certificates. Theorems H.3, H.7, H.14 and H.18 cover binary and decimal arithmetic on arbitrary nonempty operands, including unequal lengths and leading zeros. The universal certificates extend far beyond the five training programs. Theorem H.24 proves that the recovered discrete controllers implement the interpreter’s rules for arbitrary correctly encoded machines and input lengths, yielding the following consequence.

Corollary 4.2 (Exact Learning of a Universal Controller).

The universal controllers obtained by metric extraction and softmax annealing from differentiably trained DFSTs and Softmax DFSTs correctly simulate every binary Turing machine on every nonempty binary input.

GPT-6 Astra generated the proofs. We verified the arguments. The repository checkers mechanically verify finite transition obligations, while the induction arguments establish unbounded correctness.

4.3 Transferring Guarantees to Neural Controllers

Both routes transfer the recovered FST certificates to neural execution under explicit assumptions.

Graph Stability for Metric Extraction. Graph stability requires every further neural hidden-state trajectory to preserve the graph extracted from trajectories SS at threshold ε{\varepsilon}, up to state renaming.

Uniformly Bounded Leakage for Softmax DFSTs. We assume ‖ht−eqt‖1≤ε\|h_{t}-e_{q_{t}}\|_{1}\leq\varepsilon uniformly over valid inputs and execution lengths, where qtq_{t} tracks the unminimized argmax controller driven by the same observations. This bounds off-target leakage and drift from the intended one-hot state. At a one-hot hidden state, let μ\mu denote the smallest score advantage of the prescribed write or motion over any competing choice, across all valid executions. Hidden-state leakage can reduce this advantage by at most ε\varepsilon. Rounding can reduce the advantage by another 2​ρ2\rho, since each of the two compared scores can change by up to ρ\rho. Thus, μ>ε+2​ρ\mu>\varepsilon+2\rho ensures that both readouts still select the prescribed actions.

Theorem 4.3 (Behavioral Faithfulness).

Under Assumption H.1, a deterministic trace-consistent metric extraction reproduces every PTO of the neural controller on every valid input. Under Assumption G.1, the Softmax DFST and the argmax controller likewise produce identical PTOs. In either case, trace-preserving quotient reduction retains this equivalence, so an expert-equivalence certificate for the extracted controller transfers to the neural controller on the same domain.

Section H.2 proves both cases. For Softmax DFSTs, the readout margin exceeds the combined leakage and rounding perturbations, so induction preserves every action and environment update.

5 Conclusion

Our framework places differentiable parameter search inside a discrete algorithmic shell: train a neural controller, extract a discrete model through a fixed rule, and verify exact agreement with the target algorithm. Since extraction follows a fixed simple procedure (especially with argmax\argmax readout for Softmax DFSTs), we view this combination of differentiable search and discrete readout as differentiable exact learning. The certificates concern the recovered discrete models, while the graph-stability or bounded-leakage assumptions additionally transfer correctness to neural execution.

Organization of the Appendix

  • •

    Appendix A positions our work within the broader literature on neural program induction, arithmetic length generalization, and learning-theoretic supervision hierarchies.

  • •

    Appendix B proves the universality theorem for DFSTs (Theorem 2.5) and discusses non-uniqueness of DFST parametrizations.

  • •

    Appendix C collects the extended notation for grid-agent execution, the hardness results motivating our learning paradigm, the pedagogical interpretation of PTOs, and the full catalog of expert agents.

  • •

    Appendix D details optimizer settings, the learning-rate schedule, per-task DFST recipes, the recurrent-controller comparisons, and the capped evaluation protocol.

  • •

    Appendix E presents additional uniform and robust generalization results, Softmax DFST sweeps, and training dynamics for DFST, RNN, and GRU controllers on binary arithmetic.

  • •

    Appendix F describes the teleportation rune mechanics, the Turing-machine encoding, and the 10 simulated tasks used in the universal-agent experiment.

  • •

    Appendix G develops metric extraction and softmax annealing, and separates empirical evidence from the assumptions needed for neural-model equivalence.

  • •

    Appendix H proves the verification obstruction and conditional faithfulness theorem, then presents eight mathematical equivalence certificates grouped by task, including the required transition maps.

  • •

    Appendix I constructs small arithmetic controllers that match every short-input PTO yet fail beyond the training lengths, and relates these counterexamples to the Softmax DFST capacity sweeps.

Appendix A Related Work

Our work builds on a long line of research on neural program induction, which studies the problem of learning algorithmic procedures using neural architectures. Within this paradigm, prior work has explored a wide variety of learning signals and model classes. Our framework combines the following three desiderata:

  1. (1)

    Learning from expert behavior observations;

  2. (2)

    Computational universality of the learning framework;

  3. (3)

    Continuous optimization in a fully differentiable setting.

This work investigates exact learning at the intersection of these three principles, with equivalence proofs for extracted controllers over all valid inputs. Specifically, we focus on learning scenarios where intelligent systems infer algorithmic processes solely from externally observable behavior, as in learning-from-demonstration settings (Argall et al., 2009). Crucially, behavior observations circumvent the general identification barrier for input–output supervision (Gold, 1967; Papazov and Flammarion, 2025), without access to the expert’s internal state. Furthermore, we require computational universality and differentiability from our framework in order to study learning as a general-purpose mechanism, avoiding task-specific instruction templates and hand-crafted search procedures during training.

Prior universality results differ in the computational resources and learning guarantees provided:

  • ∙\bullet

    Precision and Context Requirements: RNNs and Neural GPUs with unbounded-precision internal arithmetic (Siegelmann and Sontag, 1992; Pérez et al., 2019); Transformers with growing context windows or unbounded-precision internal arithmetic (Pérez et al., 2019; Dehghani et al., 2018; Bhattamishra et al., 2020; Merrill and Sabharwal, 2023a).

  • ∙\bullet

    External-Memory Constructions: Bounded-precision recurrent controllers coupled to growing memory (Chung and Siegelmann, 2021); language models prompted with a complete production-rule system (Schuurmans et al., 2024).

  • ∙\bullet

    Horizon-Dependent Architectures: Statistical approximation guarantees for bounded-time computation with model sizes depending on the execution horizon (Wei et al., 2022).

These results establish computational expressivity or statistical approximation rather than recovery of a persistent controller from behavior observations. Finite-precision universality alone therefore does not distinguish our framework. Our universal controller instead learns from 75 PTOs without supplied control states or a transition table, transfers to five programs absent from training, and yields extracted-controller certificates covering arbitrary valid machine encodings (Appendices F and H). The certified controllers retain the same parameters across unbounded input lengths and execution horizons.

We now compare the supervision and verification guarantees of related learning frameworks.

External-Memory Frameworks. The work of Zaremba et al. (2016) comes, perhaps, closest to our setting. The authors consider an RNN-based controller which operates over a read-only input grid and a write-only unidirectional output tape by issuing action tokens containing move and write commands. Zaremba et al. (2016) investigate whether the neural controller can learn to execute simple algorithms (e.g., copying, reversing, addition) when trained via reinforcement learning for correct outputs or with supervision from expert policies. Unlike in our experiments, training uses nontrivial curricula, and off-the-shelf Q-learning fails on most tasks without additional modifications. The task suite includes single-digit multiplication and demonstrates substantial extrapolation on selected tasks. Our experiments additionally cover unrestricted two-operand multiplication and universal simulation using an unbounded read–write workspace.

Related neurosymbolic frameworks include Higher-Order RNNs (Giles et al., 1989), Memory Networks (Weston et al., 2014), Neural Turing Machines (Graves et al., 2014), Neural GPUs (Kaiser and Sutskever, 2015), Neural Random-Access Machines (Kurach et al., 2015), Neural Programmers (Neelakantan et al., 2015), Pointer Networks (Vinyals et al., 2015), Stack-Augmented RNNs (Joulin and Mikolov, 2015), Differentiable Neural Computers (Graves et al., 2016), Hierarchical Attentive Memories (Andrychowicz and Kurach, 2016), TerpreT (Gaunt et al., 2016), R3NNs (Parisotto et al., 2016), Differentiable Forth Interpreters (Bošnjak et al., 2017), and Neural-Symbolic Stack Machines (Chen et al., 2020). External storage and even unbounded differentiable memory already appear in this literature (Grefenstette et al., 2015). Our distinction concerns learning latent controller state from PTOs and certifying the extracted computation, rather than external memory alone.

Input-Output Observations. Another closely related approach appears in Zaremba and Sutskever (2015), which considers an LSTM controller operating over a read-only input tape, a read–write memory tape, and a write-only unidirectional output tape. The addition of a read–write memory renders the resulting model computationally universal. Nevertheless, learning proceeds solely via RL with rewards for correct output. Gold (1967, Theorems I.3 and I.5) rule out identification of the full class of recursive functions from input–output observations; these results do not prohibit learning a particular arithmetic algorithm. PTOs avoid this general identification barrier (Papazov and Flammarion, 2025), while the present experiments investigate finite-data optimization and verification.

Program-Structure Observations. A particularly relevant line of work stems from Neural Programmer-Interpreters (NPIs) (Reed and De Freitas, 2015). NPIs use an LSTM controller as a program executor: At each step, the controller consumes a local environment snapshot together with the active subprogram embedding and current arguments, then outputs (i) a distribution over the next subprogram in a fixed library, (ii) the corresponding arguments, and (iii) a halt/return decision. Training traces explicitly supervise this call–return structure. Each program invocation starts a fresh recurrent state; return resumes the caller’s state. These annotations expose program structure, without supplying the numerical recurrent hidden vectors.

This additional program supervision supports data-efficient learning44 4 The addition experiments train on 200 execution traces with operands of at most three digits. and in special cases permits formal guarantees of exactness. Cai et al. (2017) observe that when the expert program follows a recursive template in which each subprogram admits only finitely many base configurations and reductions, one can formally certify that the trained LSTM controller recovers the ground-truth algorithm. The experiments already reach 5000-digit addition, with all-input proofs for addition and several sorting tasks. Our distinction concerns recovering persistent controller state without prescribed subprogram identities or recursive boundaries, and extending the certificates to full binary and decimal multiplication and universal simulation. Pierrot et al. (2019) further demonstrate reinforcement learning through hierarchical program specifications, pre/postcondition checks, and recursive tree search; an induction argument certifies unbounded Tower of Hanoi execution for agents satisfying specified base-case and recursive-trace conditions. Our training instead uses PTO next-action losses without a supplied recursive decomposition or program library.

Exact Instruction Learning and Logic Induction. Back de Luca et al. (2025) prove high-probability exact instruction execution in the infinite-width neural tangent kernel regime using explicit instruction templates, but require retraining whenever the memory budget increases; neural training experiments cover permutations, while arithmetic training remains untested because of ensemble cost. Our controllers retain fixed parameters across input lengths; the extracted-controller proofs impose no memory or execution-horizon bound.

Payani and Fekri (2019) recover explicit recursive programs from positive/negative facts and supplied background predicates, including addition for multiplication, without NPI-style program-structure supervision; the empirical studies use finite domains and provide neither length-generalization measurements nor equivalence proofs over all valid inputs. Our multiplication controllers learn digit-level actions and carry propagation without a supplied addition subroutine, and admit all-input proofs after extraction.

Arithmetic Length Generalization. Finally, we situate our contribution in the arithmetic generalization literature.

Recent empirical studies (Joulin and Mikolov, 2015; Delétang et al., 2022; Liu et al., 2022; Zhang et al., 2022; Shen et al., 2023; Kazemnejad et al., 2023; Jelassi et al., 2023) demonstrate that Transformers, modified RNNs, and LSTMs length-generalize poorly on a variety of simple algorithmic tasks when trained on input-output data. With additional data-formatting strategies (such as task-specific index hints, optimized positional encodings, input reversing, position coupling, and scratchpad guidance) multiple works on arithmetic generalization in Transformers (Anil et al., 2022; Jelassi et al., 2023; H. Zhou et al., 2023; Lee et al., 2023; Y. Zhou et al., 2024; Hou et al., 2025; Cho et al., 2024a; Cho et al., 2024b) achieve substantial finite-length extrapolation. Most notably, for decimal addition, Y. Zhou et al. (2024) report above 98% exact-match accuracy (EMA) on 100-digit summands after training on decimal addition with up to 40-digit numbers (2.5×\times LG); and Cho et al. (2024a) report above 95% EMA on roughly 6–7×\times longer operands, with a separate scale-up experiment reaching 500 digits after training on operands of up to 160 digits. The clearest quantitative distinction concerns both operands in decimal multiplication: Cho et al. (2024b) train on operands of at most 10×1010\times 10 digits and attain at least 78.55% median EMA through 20×1520\times 15 digits, counting the entire response including the scratchpad, whereas Hou et al. (2025) extrapolate from 50×150\times 1 or 50×350\times 3 digits to 100×1100\times 1 or 100×3100\times 3 digits with 97% accuracy. Our selected decimal-multiplication controller trains on operands of at most 5×55\times 5 digits and passes every action-level probe at 1000×10001000\times 1000 digits before extraction; the extracted controller additionally admits a proof over all valid inputs.

Interestingly, similar to us, Hou et al. (2025) train on scratchpad data consisting of the computational traces of a Turing machine (TM) designed to solve the specific algorithmic task. However, whereas our agent only observes the evolution of the environment, Hou et al. (2025) supervise explicit machine states, head positions, and tape contents. The random-machine experiments evaluate one-step prediction on longer tapes, without establishing correct execution over unbounded trajectories. The accompanying RASP construction guarantees exp⁡(n)\exp(n) simulated steps with a program of size O⁡(n)O(n) under distinct-nn-gram and in-memory execution assumptions; this construction does not certify experimentally trained weights. Our PTOs withhold expert control states, and the extracted-controller proofs impose no input-length or execution-horizon bound.

We conclude by comparing our results in Table 1 against the Neural GPU (Kaiser and Sutskever, 2015; Price et al., 2016), which achieves strong arithmetic generalization from input-output observations. Kaiser and Sutskever (2015) introduce a Neural Cellular Automaton, called the Neural GPU, which achieves remarkable random-test generalization when trained solely on input-output examples (and an upper bound on the computation length) of binary addition and multiplication. Error-free sampled binary multiplication already reaches 2000 bits, exceeding our 1000-digit testing cap. However, Price et al. (2016) report sensitivity to the random seed and document long-carry and symmetric-input failures, despite greater than 99% whole-answer accuracy for decimal multiplication at 100 digits. Our selected models pass all repdigit cross-pairs at the testing caps in both bases, including decimal multiplication, and the extracted controllers admit proofs of exact learning. The single-seed DFST schedule sweeps do not establish superior robustness across random seeds. Furthermore, our DFST agents train on small PTO datasets using Adam, gradient clipping, and a learning-rate schedule, while Neural GPU training combines curricula, parameter-sharing relaxation, dropout, and gradient noise. As shown in Table 1, observable intermediate steps support extreme generalization with far fewer training examples, although PTOs provide richer supervision than input-output pairs. RNN and GRU runs also reach both binary-task caps, supporting the broader state-tracking recipe beyond DFSTs (Section E.3).

Summary. Our contribution combines latent-state discovery from behavior, extreme extrapolation in both arithmetic operands, and exact verification within one universal framework. Eight certificates cover extracted controllers across all five trained tasks. Graph stability or a suitable invariant of the annealed dynamics additionally transfers these guarantees to the neural controllers (Appendices G and H).

Appendix B Differentiable Finite-State Transducers

This appendix collects the formal details of DFST expressivity deferred from Section 2. We prove Theorem 2.5, discuss the non-uniqueness of emulating parametrizations, and relate the required hidden-state dimension to the number of states of the target agent.

We restate the theorem for convenience.

Softmax DFSTs under Rounded Arithmetic. For the dd-dimensional one-hot construction above, assign logit 00 to each selected coordinate and −L-L to every other coordinate. A stable softmax whose exponential rounds exp⁡(−L)\exp(-L) to zero produces exactly the required one-hot column; apply the same construction to the initial state. For example, correctly rounded binary32 exponentiation with round-to-nearest underflows exp⁡(−128)\exp(-128) to zero. Once the implementation produces these vertices and preserves the corresponding matrix–vector operations, the original induction applies unchanged for every execution length. The saturation condition concerns the effective probabilities, rather than large finite logits alone.

For Turing-completeness, observe that standard Turing machines arise as grid agents restricted to a single row of the grid. Each construction emulates every such agent under the stated arithmetic conditions, so both controller families can simulate any Turing machine. ∎

B.2 Non-Uniqueness of Emulating Parametrizations

The one-hot construction in the proof above produces one particular DFST that emulates a given grid agent TT, but many other parametrizations achieve the same behavior. In exact arithmetic, any invertible matrix R∈ℚd×dR\in{\mathbb{Q}}^{d\times d} defines an equivalent controller through

A′​[x]\displaystyle A^{\prime}[x] =R​A​[x]​R−1,\displaystyle=RA[x]R^{-1}, B′​[x]\displaystyle B^{\prime}[x] =B⁡[x]​R−1,\displaystyle=B[x]R^{-1},
C′​[x]\displaystyle C^{\prime}[x] =C⁡[x]​R−1,\displaystyle=C[x]R^{-1}, h0′\displaystyle h^{\prime}_{0} =R​h0.\displaystyle=Rh_{0}.

Induction gives ht′=R​hth^{\prime}_{t}=Rh_{t} for every read sequence, while B′​[xt]​ht−1′=B⁡[xt]​ht−1B^{\prime}[x_{t}]h^{\prime}_{t-1}=B[x_{t}]h_{t-1} and C′​[xt]​ht−1′=C⁡[xt]​ht−1C^{\prime}[x_{t}]h^{\prime}_{t-1}=C[x_{t}]h_{t-1} preserve both readouts. Thus the transformed controller reproduces every action and PTO. Choosing R=c​IdR=cI_{d} for distinct nonzero rational values cc already yields infinitely many distinct exact-arithmetic parametrizations, since h0≠0h_{0}\neq 0. These transformations preserve the PTO loss and therefore generate infinitely many zero-loss realizations of the expert’s one-hot targets.

A fixed finite arithmetic format admits only finitely many parameter configurations. Arbitrary rational changes of basis need not preserve representability or execution under rounding, so the infinitude claim does not extend to fixed finite precision. Permutations of the one-hot construction nevertheless preserve the binary weights and vertex operations, yielding equivalent finite-precision realizations whenever those operations remain exact. Separately, adding unreachable states yields infinitely many discrete grid agents with the same observable policy.

B.3 Hidden-State Dimension and State Complexity

Theorem 2.5 guarantees that an nn-dimensional ordinary DFST suffices to emulate any nn-state grid agent. Most ordinary-DFST experiments therefore match the hidden dimension to the expert state count, but successful learning does not require an exact match. For the 11-state add2 expert, a sweep over hidden dimensions d∈{5,8,11,14,17}d\in\{5,8,11,14,17\} reaches the 5000-digit RLG cap at every tested dimension except d=5d=5. Thus both a smaller controller and controllers with excess capacity achieve extreme tested generalization. These finite probes do not establish exact simulation on arbitrary inputs or identify the minimum sufficient dimension.

The Softmax DFST sweeps provide complementary evidence for the benefits of additional capacity (Figures 9 and 13). Binary addition reaches both caps with dimensions 22 and 33, compared with 11 expert states; binary multiplication reaches both caps with dimensions 64 and 96, compared with 32 expert states. Universal simulation reaches every task cap with dimensions 30 and 45, compared with 15 expert states. Across these tasks, successful configurations therefore accommodate two or three times the expert state count. Larger dimensions do not improve every configuration, but these results support choosing excess capacity when the expert state count remains unknown: precise knowledge of that count need not precede successful training.

Precisely characterizing the minimum hidden dimension required for a DFST to simulate a given nn-state FST remains an open direction. The one-hot construction supplies an upper bound of nn for ordinary DFSTs, while smaller representations may exploit the structure of the target transitions and outputs. Such a characterization should distinguish agreement on all input strings from agreement only on realizable environment traces, and account for arithmetic precision and readout margins. A separate question concerns whether gradient-based training can reliably discover representations near the minimum dimension.

Appendix C Grid Agents, PTOs, and Task Catalog

This appendix collects the pedagogical interpretation of PTOs, the formal notation for grid-agent execution, the hardness results that motivate our learning paradigm, and the full catalog of expert agents used in our experiments.

C.1 Pedagogical Interpretation of PTOs

Intelligent agents rarely acquire novel algorithmic skills from input–output pairs alone. Rather, learning typically proceeds from observing the evolution of an underlying computational process and inferring the target function from intermediate steps. The PTO formalism admits a concrete pedagogical interpretation: A grid agent models a teacher navigating a blackboard, with qtq_{t} corresponding to the teacher’s mental state, ptp_{t} marking the chalk’s position, and xt+1x_{t+1} denoting the symbol written at that position. Students observe the chalk’s movements mt+1m_{t+1} and the evolving blackboard contents st+1s_{t+1} but lack access to the teacher’s neuronal activity qt→qt+1q_{t}\to q_{t+1}. PTOs thus capture a rich but reasonable chain of thought – not unlike the algorithmic scratchpad data employed to boost length generalization in Transformers (Lee et al., 2023), yet grounded in the natural structure of agentic computation rather than requiring internal-state annotations (Hou et al., 2025; Cai et al., 2017).

C.2 Extended Notation for Grid-Agent Execution

We extend δ{\delta} and γ{\gamma} recursively to Q×Σ⋆Q\times{\Sigma^{\star}} in the standard way and denote by T⁡(x)=T⁡(x1​…​xn)T(x)=T(x_{1}\dots x_{n}) the output sequence γ⁡(q0,x1),γ⁡(δ⁡(q0,x1),x2),…,γ⁡(δ⁡(q0,x1​…​xn−1),xn){\gamma}(q_{0},x_{1}),\,{\gamma}({\delta}(q_{0},x_{1}),x_{2}),\,\dots,\,{\gamma}({\delta}(q_{0},x_{1}\dots x_{n-1}),x_{n}).

Each algorithmic task 𝒫\mathcal{P} comes with a set of well-specified inputs S𝒫⊆Σ⋆S_{\mathcal{P}}\subseteq{\Sigma^{\star}}. For arithmetic tasks, each input x∈S𝒫x\in S_{\mathcal{P}} occupies cells (0,0),…,(|x|−1,0)(0,0),\dots,(|x|-1,0) on an otherwise empty grid. Universal inputs use the program-and-tape encoding in Section F.2. We also denote the initial world-state by xx (overloading notation). Running the expert grid agent TT on xx produces a PTO T⁡[x]T[x]. We write T​{x}T\{x\} for the input trace – the sequence of symbols observed by TT during execution on xx – so that T⁡(T​{x})T(T\{x\}) gives the corresponding output trace.

For a training set S⊆S𝒫S\subseteq S_{\mathcal{P}}, we write T⁡[S]T[S] for the PTOs induced by SS and T​{S}T\{S\} for the input traces due to SS. Let I=T​{S𝒫}I=T\{S_{\mathcal{P}}\} denote the set of all realizable input traces.

C.3 Hardness of Learning from Restricted Input Traces

Since II constitutes a restricted subset of Σ⋆{\Sigma^{\star}}, a training set SS – no matter how large – may leave some transitions of TT unexplored. This incompleteness makes the learning problem fundamentally hard: Many irreducible FSTs can exhibit identical behavior on II.

Learning FSTs from complete data constitutes a classical problem in grammatical inference, enjoying polynomial-size characteristic sets (Gold, 1978; Oncina and Garcia, 1992; De La Higuera, 1997; Parekh and Honavar, 2001) and efficient active-learning algorithms (Angluin, 1987; Vaandrager et al., 2022). However, restricting all observable inputs to the unknown set II dramatically increases difficulty. In particular, Papazov and Flammarion (2025, Theorem 17) proved that no polynomial-size characteristic set exists for this restricted problem, implying that no algorithm can learn the policy of every grid agent from polynomially many PTOs with lengths polynomial in the number of states of the expert agent.

C.4 Expert Agent Catalog

Table 2 summarizes the state counts, alphabets, and runtimes of all grid agents and Turing machines used in our experiments. For arithmetic tasks, mm and nn denote the lengths in digits of the two operands; for all other tasks, nn denotes the input length.

For universal simulation, QMQ_{M} denotes the state set of the simulated Turing machine MM, including the halting state, and |M⁡[z]||M[z]| counts the simulated machine’s actions on input zz, including the stopping action. The runtime bound counts each teleportation as one action.

The public controller walkthrough provides animated expert executions and instructions for inspecting individual computation steps.

Appendix D Implementation and Experimental Details

We specify the data, optimization, execution semantics, and evaluation protocol for the experiments. Appendix A compares these results with prior work.

The public repository provides training recipes, saved model weights and run configurations, and commands for reproducing the figures and analyses.

D.1 Data and Controller Initialization

Arithmetic training uses small PTO datasets from distinct operand-string pairs, retaining leading zeros. Each set includes all single-digit pairs. Remaining pairs follow independent uniform sampling of each operand length from 1,…,q1,\ldots,q and of each digit from 0,…,R−10,\ldots,R-1, with duplicate pairs rejected. The ordinary-DFST datasets contain 25, 250, 100, and 10 000 PTOs for add2, add10, mult2, and mult10, respectively. Addition uses q=3q=3 and multiplication uses q=5q=5. These experiments use the ordinary sampler without an additional teaching-set coverage core. The plotted DFST and Softmax DFST sweeps use data seed 42. Separately, we replicated strong length generalization across three data-generation seeds using the same deterministic initialization recipe.

Minibatch sampling chooses uniformly among occupied operand-length buckets, then uniformly among PTOs within the chosen bucket. Universal training first chooses a represented training task uniformly once per minibatch, then samples length buckets within that task. Consequently, training does not sample uniformly over all stored PTOs.

Ordinary DFSTs start from A⁡[x]=IdA[x]=I_{d}, B⁡[x]=0B[x]=0, C⁡[x]=0C[x]=0, and a trainable h0=𝟏dh_{0}=\mathbf{1}_{d}. In the ordinary-DFST schedule sweeps, hidden dimensions match the experts: 11, 19, 32, and 108 for the four arithmetic tasks, and 15 for universal simulation. Inputs use frozen one-hot embeddings. The resulting arithmetic controllers contain 891, 8227, 5280, and 162 108 trainable parameters, respectively. Training uses float32 arithmetic and logarithmic-depth prefix scans.

All DFST and Softmax DFST models begin PTO training from scratch without a pretrained checkpoint. Softmax DFSTs initialize the transition logits to IdI_{d}, output logits to zero, and initial-state logits to 𝟏d\mathbf{1}_{d}, then apply softmax normalization. Consequently, the effective initial state and output columns start uniformly, while transition columns favor the identity successor. Ordinary and softmax universal controllers contain 4335 and 12 720 trainable parameters at dimensions 15 and 30, respectively.

D.2 Optimizer and Learning-Rate Schedule

Ordinary DFST training uses Adam (Kingma, 2014) with (β1,β2)=(0.9,0.999)(\beta_{1},\beta_{2})=(0.9,0.999), ϵ=10−8\epsilon=10^{-8}, zero weight decay, batch size 32, and global gradient-norm clipping at 1. Let TT denote the update budget, ω\omega the warm-up duration, cc the constant-rate duration, γ\gamma the peak rate, and γf\gamma_{f} the floor, with ω+c<T\omega+c<T. The schedule follows

γ⁡(t)={γf1−t/ω​γt/ω,0≤t<ω,γ,ω≤t<ω+c,γ1−(t−ω−c)/(T−ω−c)​γf(t−ω−c)/(T−ω−c),ω+c≤t≤T.\gamma(t)=\begin{cases}\gamma_{f}^{1-t/\omega}\gamma^{t/\omega},&0\leq t<\omega,\\[2.0pt] \gamma,&\omega\leq t<\omega+c,\\[2.0pt] \gamma^{1-(t-\omega-c)/(T-\omega-c)}\gamma_{f}^{(t-\omega-c)/(T-\omega-c)},&\omega+c\leq t\leq T.\end{cases} (1)

A zero-duration phase contributes no updates. The DFST sweeps use c=0c=0; GRU dynamics include the plateaus in Table 5. Updates use t=0,…,T−1t=0,\ldots,T-1; the endpoint at TT equals the floor. Within the DFST sweeps, binary arithmetic uses γ=10−2\gamma=10^{-2}; decimal arithmetic and universal simulation use γ=10−3\gamma=10^{-3}. The DFST sweeps use γf=10−7\gamma_{f}=10^{-7}; the separate multiplication dynamics run uses 10−910^{-9}.

D.3 Loss and Training Loop

For a minibatch, let MtM_{t} mask valid timesteps and let 𝟏st\mathbf{1}_{s_{t}} and 𝟏mt\mathbf{1}_{m_{t}} encode the expert write and motion actions. The masked two-head MSE reads

ℒ=∑tMt​(‖s^t−𝟏st‖22+‖m^t−𝟏mt‖22)2​∑tMt.{\mathcal{L}}=\frac{\sum_{t}M_{t}\bigl(\|\hat{s}_{t}-\mathbf{1}_{s_{t}}\|_{2}^{2}+\|\hat{m}_{t}-\mathbf{1}_{m_{t}}\|_{2}^{2}\bigr)}{2\sum_{t}M_{t}}. (2)

The sum extends over the batch and time axes. Padding contributes neither recurrent updates nor loss. Training feeds expert observations into the controller and supervises the next write and motion. The ordinary-DFST runs use no curriculum, inverse-frequency weighting, or extraction during optimization. Logged losses average the action objective over updates in each logging window. The training-dynamics figure averages loss over 1000 updates and evaluates saved checkpoints every 100 000 updates.

D.4 Softmax DFST Training

The probability parametrization in Appendix G replaces each transition and output column by a softmax distribution and normalizes the initial state. The initial training sweep uses 100 000 Adam updates at constant learning rate 0.10.1, MSE, batch size 32, gradient clipping at 1, and zero regularization weight. For add2, dimensions {11,22,33}\{11,22,33\} combine with dataset sizes {25,50,75}\{25,50,75\}; for mult2, dimensions {32,64,96}\{32,64,96\} combine with sizes {100,200,300}\{100,200,300\}. Universal simulation uses dimensions {15,30,45}\{15,30,45\} and sizes {75,150,225}\{75,150,225\}. The later annealing stage follows the separate procedure in Appendix G. Neither the softmax sweep nor annealing shares the ordinary-DFST learning-rate schedule by default.

D.5 Additional State-Tracking Controllers

All controller families receive the currently observed symbol and emit separate write and motion scores. RNN and GRU heads act on the post-update hidden vector; DFST heads act on the previous vector together with the current observation. An Elman RNN uses

ht=tanh⁡(Wx​xt+Wh​ht−1+b),s^t=Ws​ht+bs,m^t=Wm​ht+bm.h_{t}=\tanh(W_{x}x_{t}+W_{h}h_{t-1}+b),\qquad\hat{s}_{t}=W_{s}h_{t}+b_{s},\quad\hat{m}_{t}=W_{m}h_{t}+b_{m}.

GRU controllers replace the recurrence by gated reset, update, and candidate-state operations while retaining the same action heads. All recurrent baselines use one layer and frozen one-hot input embeddings. The RNN addition run initializes recurrent weights orthogonally, input weights with Xavier initialization, and recurrent biases to zero, with a fixed zero initial state. The RNN multiplication run and both GRU runs use zero input weights, zero recurrent biases, and a trainable all-ones initial state. For RNN multiplication, the recurrent matrix starts at the identity. For GRUs, only the candidate-state recurrent block starts at the identity; reset- and update-gate recurrent blocks start at zero. All RNN and GRU action heads use the linear layers’ default random initialization.

Addition controllers contain 891, 1513, and 3977 trainable parameters for DFST, RNN, and GRU, respectively; multiplication controllers contain 5280, 5129, and 14089. Each addition dataset contains 25 PTOs with operands of at most three digits; each multiplication dataset contains 100 PTOs with operands of at most five digits. The different seeds produce different datasets within the same sampling recipe. Consequently, the training histories demonstrate successful learning across controller families without isolating architecture from initialization, data, and optimization choices.

D.6 Length-Generalization Evaluation

Every probe streams an expert PTO and requires the predicted write and motion to match at every real timestep, including the single final stopping action. ULG tests ten uniformly sampled pairs with both operands of exactly LL digits. RLG additionally tests all R2R^{2} repdigit pairs (aL,bL)(a^{L},b^{L}) with a,b∈{0,…,R−1}a,b\in\{0,\ldots,R-1\}: four pairs for binary arithmetic and 100 for decimal arithmetic. A deterministic generator indexed by the evaluation seed, task, and candidate length fixes random probes independently of the search history.

The search first tests the cap: 5000 digits for addition, 1000 for multiplication, and 500 input symbols for universal simulation. A successful cap probe terminates the search. Otherwise, binary search probes smaller lengths; RLG cannot exceed the measured ULG. Binary search assumes monotone pass/fail behavior with length and does not exhaustively test every shorter length. Consequently, reported values describe the implemented search, and the notation ≥Lmax\geq L_{\max} records a successful capped test, not an exact maximal horizon or a mathematical guarantee for all shorter inputs.

Evaluation uses batches of at most ten expert streams, chunks of 8192 transitions, and continuation state across chunks. Ordinary DFST evaluations, including the training-dynamics runs, use parallel matrix scans; the initial softmax evaluations use sequential recurrence. RNN and GRU evaluations retain the native recurrent implementation with continuation states across chunks, even when the shared evaluation configuration records the parallel scan option. These choices matter under finite precision: parallel and sequential products can differ through rounding, and ordinary-DFST sequential stabilization rescales hidden states while the parallel path uses unscaled products. All statements about agreement concern the recorded execution mode. Extraction and the conditional transfer arguments require the corresponding execution semantics rather than an unqualified interchange of numerical implementations.

Teacher Forcing and Closed-Loop Agreement. For a deterministic recurrent execution rule and environment, exact next-action agreement along the complete expert PTO implies identical closed-loop execution on that input: induction gives the same environment, next observation, and controller history after every matching action. Floating-point parallel scans require additional care because the arithmetic association can differ from a stepwise rollout. We report the actual teacher-forced exact-match protocol and treat the autonomous extracted-FST equivalence proofs separately.

Compute Reporting. The released configurations specify CUDA execution on single NVIDIA A100-SXM4- 40GB and Tesla V100-SXM2-32GB GPUs.

D.7 Optimization Limitations and Dataset Coverage

The ordinary-DFST sweep reaches the RLG cap in five of nine add2, three of nine mult2, five of nine add10, and two of nine mult10 configurations. Additional updates need not improve RLG, and low training loss alone does not certify algorithmic correctness. The results demonstrate successful configurations across tasks and parametrizations, without asserting success for every schedule or seed.

Our Softmax DFST training attempts on decimal addition and multiplication failed to fit even very small training datasets. The softmax distributions quickly saturate, gradients vanish, and learning stalls, consistent with convergence to a poor local minimum. These failures concern fitting the training examples, before length generalization or extraction. Developing a robust training procedure for larger Softmax DFST controllers remains an open direction for future experiments.

Dataset coverage also affects generalization. Without guaranteed transition coverage, finite random sampling can omit a reachable expert transition with nonzero probability, leaving the corresponding behavior unrepresented in the training PTOs. An important research direction concerns identifying minimal teaching sets that cover all reachable expert transitions and provide sufficient information for exact learning and extreme length generalization. Transition coverage alone need not distinguish the expert from every alternative controller, so this objective also requires understanding which execution contexts resolve behavioral ambiguities. Our repository implements preliminary teaching sets that exercise all reachable transitions of the task experts, but we have not yet evaluated these sets for neural-controller training.

The released training histories include loss logs, run configurations, and checkpoint evaluations for all six runs below.
