Appendix F Universal-Agent Experiments

The universal expert uses 15 states, a nine-symbol alphabet, and eight motion tokens. A single learned controller receives the encoded program through the environment; no controller weights change between simulated tasks.

F.1 Teleportation Runes

The controller observes only the symbol under the grid head and emits a symbol to write and a motion token. The environment applies the write before the motion. The alphabet contains {λ,0,1,𝙻,𝚁,𝚂,X,Y,Z}\{{\lambda},0,1,\mathtt{L},\mathtt{R},\mathtt{S},X,Y,Z\}; motions comprise {L,R,U,D,S,X,Y,Z}\{L,R,U,D,S,X,Y,Z\}, with SS stopping execution. The three symbols X,Y,ZX,Y,Z provide relocatable bookmarks. Writing a rune stores the symbol underneath the rune at the current cell. Rewriting the same rune restores the hidden symbol at the previous location and relocates the bookmark. A motion token XX, YY, or ZZ jumps directly to the corresponding bookmark; writing a rune alone does not trigger a jump. Jumping to an unplaced rune leaves the head in place; valid simulations place each bookmark before use. Ordinary writes overwrite the current cell and remove any rune occupying that cell. The simulation relation must therefore track both visible grid contents and hidden symbols beneath runes.

During simulation, ZZ marks the simulated tape head, XX identifies the program-table block for the current simulated state, and YY bookmarks the instruction currently undergoing decoding. These operations shorten transport between the program and tape while preserving a finite controller and an unbounded environment.

F.2 Program Encoding

For a binary Turing machine with ss states, including the halting state, choose ternary width κ=max⁡{1,⌈log3⁡s⌉}\kappa=\max\{1,\lceil\log_{3}s\rceil\}. Encode state indices using 𝙻,𝚁,𝚂\mathtt{L},\mathtt{R},\mathtt{S} for ternary digits 0, 1, 2. Order program-table rows lexicographically by state index and read symbol, with blank preceding 0 and 1. Each row contains

[x,λ,code⁡(q), 0,code⁡(q′), 0,w,m],[\,x,\ {\lambda},\ \operatorname{code}(q),\ 0,\ \operatorname{code}(q^{\prime}),\ 0,\ w,\ m\,],

where (q′,w,m)(q^{\prime},w,m) denotes the Turing-machine transition on (q,x)(q,x). The two delimiter zeros separate state fields. State codes use most-significant trits first. Thus the table contains 3​s3s rows and 2​κ+62\kappa+6 columns, with three consecutive rows per state. Unoccupied grid cells contain blanks. For example, with s=3s=3, a transition (q,x)=(0,1)↦(2,0,R)(q,x)=(0,1)\mapsto(2,0,R) contributes the row [1,λ,𝙻,0,𝚂,0,0,𝚁][1,{\lambda},\mathtt{L},0,\mathtt{S},0,0,\mathtt{R}]. Initially, XX covers the blank in column 1 of the first program row. The input word occupies columns starting at 1 of the row below the program table, and the universal head starts at the first input symbol.

The controller starts in state 0. Each simulated step first records the tape-head position with ZZ and jumps to XX. A vertical search within the current-state block selects the row matching the read symbol. The controller then crosses the current-state code and decodes the next-state code one trit at a time: YY bookmarks the instruction field, while XX advances through matching state-code columns using vertical searches. After locating the successor-state block, the controller returns XX to column 1, reads the write symbol and motion through YY, and jumps to ZZ to execute the tape action. A simulated SS action performs the specified write and stops the universal controller. Rune relocation restores covered program symbols, allowing repeated interpretation of the same table without changing controller weights. The metric-extraction equivalence result in Appendix H covers correctly encoded programs and nonempty binary input words. The annealed controller also admits the empty word; the two theorem domains remain distinct.

The simulation requires O⁡(|QM|​|M⁡[z]|)O(|Q_{M}|\,|M[z]|) actions, where QMQ_{M} denotes the state set of MM, including the halting state, and |M⁡[z]||M[z]| counts the actions of MM on zz, including the stopping action. Each teleportation counts as one action.

F.3 Training and Evaluation Programs

Training samples 75, 150, or 225 PTOs with input lengths at most five from five programs: parity, shift-left, shift-right, scaling-A(5), and scaling-B(5). Static sampling includes at least one example from each training program and fills the remaining slots by random task and input sampling. The implemented sampler permits empty words, although the metric-extraction equivalence theorem restricts the unbounded claim to nonempty words.

Evaluation includes all five training families and five held-out programs: bit inversion (flip), prefix parity (cum-sum), parity-dependent bit deletion (bit-delete), reversal, and copying. The last two programs require repeated scans over growing tape regions. The scaling tests set the program parameter to the candidate input length, so evaluation at 500 increases both input length and encoded machine size. scaling-A(s) executes ss nonhalting steps followed by one stopping action; scaling-B(s) follows a parity-dependent walk through a finite chain of states. These families test new program sizes as well as longer inputs.

Table 7 summarizes the implemented programs. Alternatively, readers can inspect animated executions through the public controller-animation notebook or the animation command, for example del animate tp:copy ’1011’.

For scaling-A(s)(s), step i=0,…,s−1i=0,\ldots,s-1 maps 00 to 11 and moves left, or maps 11 to 00 and moves right. On a blank, step ii writes (i+1)mod2(i+1)\bmod 2 and moves left for even ii, right for odd ii. For scaling-B(s)(s), initialize parity p=0p=0 and direction right. Reading a bit bb writes p⊕bp\mathbin{\oplus}b and updates pp to that value; reading a blank writes pp and reverses the direction for the next step. Each nonfinal step moves in the direction held before the read; step ss writes and stops.

F.4 Generalization across Training Configurations

Figure 13 collects every evaluated universal configuration across all ten tasks. All three ordinary-DFST runs with 500k updates reach the 500-symbol cap on every task. At 250k updates, the runs reach the cap on eight, eight, and nine tasks for N=75,150,225N=75,150,225, respectively. The remaining failures involve reversal, copying, or the second scaling family.

For Softmax DFSTs, two of nine configurations reach the cap on all ten tasks after 100k updates: (d,N)=(30,150)(d,N)=(30,150) and (45,75)(45,75). Several other configurations succeed on all eight fixed programs but fail on at least one scaling family. Thus generalization across fixed programs does not guarantee extrapolation in encoded machine size, and increasing dimension or dataset size does not uniformly improve the outcome.

F.5 PTO Lengths at the Evaluation Caps

Operand length understates the execution horizon. Direct replay of the expert transition maps gives 50 070 010 PTO steps for adding two 5000-digit copies of the maximal digit and 15 012 991 steps for multiplying two 1000-digit copies, in both radix 2 and radix 10. These counts include exactly one stopping action. The maximal-digit examples belong to the evaluated repdigit family. The counts describe expert trajectories used by the cap probes; the counts do not constitute additional neural-model evaluations.

For universal simulation, replaying the ten deterministic evaluation inputs at length 500 for each task gives the maxima below. The longest sampled trajectory contains 15 316 822 steps, for copying. Thus a successful 500-symbol probe can require more than fifteen million consecutive action matches.

Appendix G Extracting Interpretable Finite-State Controllers

A trained recurrent controller already induces a finite-state machine under fixed finite-precision execution. Extraction seeks a compact description of the learned policy, suitable for interpretation and mathematical verification. We use two complementary constructions: metric extraction groups hidden states with similar geometry; annealing encourages a Softmax DFST to approach deterministic transitions. Neither construction uses expert hidden-state labels. The equivalence proofs in Appendix H concern the resulting discrete controllers. Transferring those proofs to the neural controllers requires the additional conditions stated below.

Executable notebooks accompany both metric extraction and annealing, with saved cases and instructions for analyzing another trained checkpoint.

G.1 Metric Extraction from DFST Trajectories

Autonomous Trajectory Collection. Fix a trained controller with hidden-state update fxf_{x} and decoded action gxg_{x}, where x∈Σx\in\Sigma and gx​(h)∈Σ×ℳg_{x}(h)\in\Sigma\times{\mathcal{M}}. For a DFST, fx​(h)=A​[x]​hf_{x}(h)=A[x]h and

gx​(h)=(argmaxB​[x]​h,argmaxC​[x]​h).g_{x}(h)=\bigl(\argmax B[x]h,\;\argmax C[x]h\bigr).

The readouts use the hidden state before the transition. From each sampled valid initial environment zz, run the neural controller autonomously: the predicted write and movement determine the next observation. Record

(ht−1,xt,st,mt,ht),1≤t≤L⁡(z).(h_{t-1},x_{t},s_{t},m_{t},h_{t}),\qquad 1\leq t\leq L(z).

Thus extraction observes the controller’s actual policy rather than a teacher-forced continuation after an erroneous action. A stopping action contributes the final PTO triple exactly once. Nonfinite states and runs exceeding the collection budget trigger failure rather than a fictitious halt. The metric case studies use the unrescaled sequential DFST recurrence during collection; any transfer claim refers to the same arithmetic and execution convention.

Geometric Grouping and Deterministic Closure. For a finite trajectory collection, connect two nonterminal hidden-state occurrences whenever the Euclidean distance does not exceed ε{\varepsilon}. Take the connected components of this proximity graph. Connectedness permits chains of nearby points; a component need not have diameter at most ε{\varepsilon}. For each component qq and observation xx, inspect all recorded transitions. Conflicting write–movement pairs invalidate the threshold. Otherwise, merge the successor components whenever the same pair (q,x)(q,x) reaches several successors, and repeat the consistency check and successor merging. Keep a distinguished halt state separate from nonterminal components; a required halt/nonhalt merger also invalidates the threshold. Every successful merger reduces the finite component count, so closure either terminates with a deterministic graph or detects a conflict. In the accepted graph G⁡(S,ε)G(S,{\varepsilon}), an unobserved state–symbol pair remains undefined.

Threshold selection uses the complete extraction sample before measuring graph stability. Starting from a proposed ε{\varepsilon}, halve the threshold after a conflict and restart from the original observations. The implementation permits 65 positive-threshold attempts followed by a zero-threshold attempt; an unresolved conflict aborts extraction. A successful threshold supplies consistency with the collected trajectories, without certifying behavior beyond those trajectories.

Exact Quotient Reduction. Redirect stopping transitions to a single halt node, preserving the written symbol. Conventional halt self-loops only describe behavior after execution has stopped. Apply Hopcroft partition refinement to the resulting partial Mealy transducer, distinguishing final status, output labels, and definedness. Two states can share a quotient class only when every symbol has matching definedness and, for each defined transition, matching outputs and successor classes. The quotient therefore preserves all defined traces and all missing transitions. This reduction differs from completing unknown transitions or merging states merely because the observed samples fail to distinguish the states. The case studies additionally check the quotient map transition by transition and replay every extraction trajectory.

What Graph Stability Requires. At the accepted threshold, add trajectories one at a time and compare the rooted, input/output-labeled graphs up to state renaming. The comparison preserves the initial state, halt status, missing edges, and every transition label. Equal numbers of nodes and edges alone do not establish graph identity. In the five case studies, the final unchanged suffix begins at sample 4, 42, 143, 1,870, and 23 for add2, mult2, add10, mult10, and universal, respectively. Figure 14 displays the corresponding finite observations.

Assumption H.1 requires substantially more: every finite enlargement of the sample by valid executions must preserve the same rooted labeled graph. For a nonhalting universal computation, the requirement extends to every finite execution prefix. A finite plateau provides evidence for this assumption, never a proof. Under the assumption, every valid neural trajectory follows a path already represented by the stable graph. Trace-preserving quotient reduction then transfers the neural policy to the compact controller, as formalized in Theorem 4.3. The assumption must refer to the deployed recurrence, rounding convention, and state normalization; changing those conventions requires a corresponding argument.

The phrase exponential annealing refers to the regularization schedule, not to a softmax-temperature schedule.

Reading Out the Discrete Controller. For each hidden coordinate jj and symbol xx, set

Under Assumption G.1, the neural controller and T^\widehat{T} produce identical PTOs on all valid inputs, including simultaneous stopping and every finite prefix of a nonhalting execution. Any trace-preserving quotient inherits this equivalence.

≥μ−‖h−eq‖1≥μ−ε.\displaystyle\geq\mu-\|h-e_{q}\|_{1}\geq\mu-\varepsilon.

Thus both implemented heads choose the prescribed actions on the supplied observation stream.

Now compare autonomous executions. Initially, both controllers receive the same grid, head position, and rune records. If all earlier actions agree, both environments supply xt+1​(z)x_{t+1}(z), and the deterministic neural implementation reaches the same ht​(z)h_{t}(z) as on the supplied stream. The margin argument gives the same write and motion, preserving the environment correspondence. A stopping action terminates both executions; otherwise induction continues. This proves agreement through every finite prefix and simultaneous stopping. Trace-preserving quotient reduction retains every such PTO. ∎

Sharp readout columns allow a larger tolerance for hidden-state leakage. For example, if every prescribed entry exceeds 1−β1-\beta and every competing entry remains below β\beta, then μ>1−2​β\mu>1-2\beta. Uniform leakage bounds concern the entire recurrent execution, whereas column sharpness concerns individual parameters. Exact one-hot tensors and initialization satisfy Assumption G.1 with ε=ρ=0\varepsilon=\rho=0 whenever the implemented arithmetic preserves vertex operations.

Evidence and Proof Play Different Roles. The saved finite checks for metric binary addition, binary multiplication, decimal addition, and universal simulation, and for all three annealed controllers, each report 100 exact PTO matches on 100 inputs of length 100. Arithmetic checks use two length-100 operands; universal checks sample length-100 binary words and task instances. These checks compare the extracted controller against the expert. The neural length-generalization experiments in Section 3 provide separate evidence before extraction. Neither evidence source replaces the inductive proofs in Appendix H, and neither proves Assumptions H.1 and G.1. The eight proofs establish exact algorithmic learning for the extracted controllers; the stated graph-stability or bounded-leakage assumptions transfer the corresponding conclusion to the trained neural controllers.

Appendix H Proving Exact Learning

LLM Assistance. We used GPT-6 Astra to generate the controller-equivalence proofs and verified the arguments ourselves. Executable certificate checkers validate the finite transition obligations; the unbounded equivalence claims additionally rely on the mathematical invariants and induction arguments presented below. We take responsibility for the correctness of the final statements and proofs.

We separate three claims: equality of sampled PTOs, exact equivalence of an extracted controller, and transfer of that equivalence to the trained neural controller. The proofs below establish the second claim without a length bound. Transfer requires the graph-stability or bounded-leakage assumptions discussed in Section 4; finite experiments alone establish neither assumption.

The public proof bundles supply machine-readable transition maps and executable checks of the finite certificate obligations. The arguments below establish the unbounded claims independently of the accompanying code.

H.1 Why Finite Testing Cannot Certify General Equivalence

With fixed weights and deterministic arithmetic, DD recurrent scalars stored in bb bits induce at most 2b​D2^{bD} memory encodings. Restricting each scalar to a finite IEEE binary32 value gives (232−224)D(2^{32}-2^{24})^{D} encodings, counting signed zeros separately. Here D=dD=d for DFSTs, Softmax DFSTs, RNNs, and GRUs. This enormous FST remains difficult to inspect; ordinary FST equivalence on arbitrary read strings does not resolve equivalence under an unbounded environment.

Proof of Lemma 4.1.

Suppose an algorithm computes the claimed horizon. Given a Turing machine NN and input ww, construct two grid agents that simulate exactly |z||z| steps of N⁡(w)N(w) on input zz, using identical visible actions throughout the simulation. If the simulation detects halting, the agents emit different final actions; otherwise both agents stop with the same PTO. Every such execution terminates. The agents agree on every input precisely when N⁡(w)N(w) never halts. A computed horizon would reduce this universal equivalence claim to finitely many terminating comparisons, deciding nonhalting and therefore halting. This contradiction proves the claim. The obstruction concerns controllers interacting with an unbounded environment; ordinary finite-state transducer equivalence on unrestricted read strings remains decidable. ∎

H.2 Transferring an Extracted Certificate to a Trained Controller

Let G⁡(S,ε)G(S,{\varepsilon}) denote the deterministic, trace-consistent graph extracted from valid neural executions SS at threshold ε{\varepsilon}, including finite prefixes of nonhalting executions.

Assumption H.1 (Graph Stability).

For some ε>0{\varepsilon}>0 and finite sample SS, every finite extension S′S^{\prime} by valid neural execution traces or prefixes yields a successful extraction and a graph G⁡(S′,ε)G(S^{\prime},{\varepsilon}) isomorphic to G⁡(S,ε)G(S,{\varepsilon}), preserving the root, read symbols, output labels, and stopping actions.

Proof of Theorem 4.3.

For metric extraction, fix a valid input and any finite execution prefix of the trained controller. Extend the extraction data by that prefix. Trace consistency embeds every observed transition into the resulting graph. Graph stability identifies the extended rooted, input/output-labeled graph with the original graph, including the initial node and stopping convention. Thus the original graph reproduces every action of the prefix. Induction synchronizes the controller and graph: equal grids and head positions provide equal read symbols; equal output labels produce equal writes and motions and preserve the next configuration. Rune records, when present, evolve identically under the same actions. Since the argument permits every prefix length, the complete finite PTOs agree, or every finite prefix agrees for a nonterminating execution. Any subsequent merging that preserves all defined traces preserves this conclusion. Composing this equality with an extracted-controller certificate proves equivalence to the expert. Equality of node or edge counts alone would not supply the labeled-graph identity used in this argument. For Softmax DFSTs, Proposition G.2 establishes equality of every finite PTO prefix under Assumption G.1. Trace-preserving reduction and composition with the expert-equivalence certificate give the same conclusion. ∎

H.3 A Common Simulation Principle

Write ℰ\mathcal{E} for an expert and 𝒞\mathcal{C} for an extracted controller. A transition δ⁡(q,x)=(q′,w,M)\delta(q,x)=(q^{\prime},w,M) reads xx, writes ww, performs motion MM, and enters state q′q^{\prime}. Motion SS writes and stops without moving. PTOs contain read/write/motion triples and count the final stopping action once; halt loops contribute no additional observations. Arithmetic inputs occupy row 00 from column 00, with all other cells blank and the head initially at (0,0)(0,0). Arithmetic coordinates increase rightward and downward. Operand words may have unequal positive lengths and leading zeros.

A phase records the expert control state together with finite geometric or arithmetic context. A phase need not correspond to a distinct machine state. The following lemma explains why a finite certificate can establish equality of arbitrarily long executions.

Lemma H.2 (Phase Simulation).

Suppose a protocol covers every valid expert execution. Assign expert state gig_{i} and a nonempty controller-state set QiQ_{i} to each phase ii. Assume the initial states belong to the initial phase relation. For each permitted edge i→𝑥ji\xrightarrow{x}j and every q∈Qiq\in Q_{i}, suppose

δℰ​(gi,x)=(gj,w,M),δ𝒞​(q,x)=(q′,w,M),q′∈Qj.\delta_{\mathcal{E}}(g_{i},x)=(g_{j},w,M),\qquad\delta_{\mathcal{C}}(q,x)=(q^{\prime},w,M),\qquad q^{\prime}\in Q_{j}. (11)

Assume stopping occurs exactly on edges to terminal phases. Then the two controllers produce identical PTOs on the valid input domain, with identical environment configurations at every step.

Proof.

Relate configurations with the same grid, head, and, where applicable, rune records, and control states gig_{i} and q∈Qiq\in Q_{i}. Initially this relation holds. Protocol coverage provides an allowed read symbol; equal configurations provide the same symbol to both controllers. Equation (11) gives the same write and motion and relates the successor states. The deterministic environment update preserves the relation. Induction proves equality of every finite prefix. The stopping condition gives simultaneous termination, or equal infinite PTOs. No undefined transition can occur along a valid execution. ∎

Multivalued QiQ_{i} capture different internal realizations of the same phase. Each listed branch applies to every state in the corresponding set. Undefined or unlisted branches require no completion when the coverage proof excludes those branches. Local identities can therefore be checked by finite substitution, while the geometric invariants supply the unbounded claim.

H.4 Binary Addition: Two Certificates, One Arithmetic Invariant

Let D={0,1}D=\{0,1\} and consider a+ba+b with a∈Dma\in D^{m}, b∈Dnb\in D^{n}, m,n≥1m,n\geq 1. Write A=val2⁡(a)A=\operatorname{val}_{2}(a) and B=val2⁡(b)B=\operatorname{val}_{2}(b). The expert starts in state 00 and halts in state 1010. The metric and annealed controllers start in state 00 and halt in states 2121 and 1616, respectively.

Theorem H.3 (Exact Binary Addition).

Both extracted controllers produce the expert PTO on every valid binary-addition input, with identical grids and head positions at every step.

H.4.1 Shared Expert Behavior and Observation Protocol

Accumulator and Marker Invariant

Write B=∑j=0n−1bj​2jB=\sum_{j=0}^{n-1}b_{j}2^{j}, with b0b_{0} the rightmost digit. The expert scans to the separator at column mm, steps left and down, writes a working ++ below column m−1m-1, and enters state 88 above the marker.

Lemma H.4 (Round Invariant).

After processing kk right-operand digits, 0≤k≤n0\leq k\leq n, the expert enters state 88 at (pk,0)(p_{k},0), where pk=m−1−kp_{k}=m-1-k. At this point:

  • •

    Row 11 contains exactly one nonblank symbol: a ++ at column pkp_{k}.

  • •

    Row 00 contains a contiguous accumulator on [ℓk,m−1][\ell_{k},m-1], with value Ck=A+∑j<kbj​2jC_{k}=A+\sum_{j<k}b_{j}2^{j} and left edge ℓk≤pk+1\ell_{k}\leq p_{k}+1. Column m−1m-1 carries the units digit.

  • •

    The separator remains at column mm. The unprocessed prefix of bb occupies columns m+1,…,m+n−km+1,\ldots,m+n-k. All remaining cells contain blanks.

Proof.

Initialization gives k=0k=0, ℓ0=0\ell_{0}=0, C0=AC_{0}=A, and p0=m−1p_{0}=m-1. State 88 preserves the digit at pkp_{k}, or writes 00 on a blank. A blank at pkp_{k} forces ℓk=pk+1\ell_{k}=p_{k}+1, so zero extension preserves contiguity.

For k<nk<n, the right scan reaches the blank after the unprocessed prefix, steps left to digit bkb_{k} at rk=m+n−kr_{k}=m+n-k, erases bkb_{k}, and descends. The expert transports bkb_{k} left along row 11 to the marker. The distance satisfies

rk−pk=n+1≥2.r_{k}-p_{k}=n+1\geq 2. (12)

Consequently, the first two transport steps read blanks. At the marker, the expert ascends and adds bkb_{k} to the accumulator digit ee at column pkp_{k}. If e+bk<2e+b_{k}<2, the expert writes e+bke+b_{k} and descends. Otherwise, the expert writes e+bk−2e+b_{k}-2, moves left, and propagates one carry. Each digit 11 changes to 00; the first smaller digit increases by one, or a blank changes to 11. The update adds exactly bk​2kb_{k}2^{k} and preserves contiguity.

The expert returns along row 11, erases the marker, steps left, writes the next marker at pk+1=pk−1p_{k+1}=p_{k}-1, and ascends into state 88. The earlier zero extension gives ℓk+1≤pk=pk+1+1\ell_{k+1}\leq p_{k}=p_{k+1}+1. The accumulator now has value Ck+1C_{k+1}, establishing the next round. ∎

Lemma H.5 (Termination and Final Configuration).

The expert terminates with only the padded base-22 representation of A+BA+B on row 00, ending at column m−1m-1. The final head stops at (m−n−1,0)(m-n-1,0). Writing ℓ2​(s)\ell_{2}(s) for the binary digit count, with ℓ2​(0)=1\ell_{2}(0)=1, the output width equals L=max⁡{m,n+1,ℓ2​(A+B)}L=\max\{m,n+1,\ell_{2}(A+B)\}.

Proof.

Each round consumes one of the nn right-operand digits. Every scan crosses a finite interval, and every carry reaches a digit below 11 or a blank. After round nn, state 88 ensures a digit at pnp_{n}. The next right scan returns to the separator. State 33 erases the separator and descends. State 99 walks left, erases the final marker, ascends, preserves the accumulator digit, and stops. The invariant gives Cn=A+BC_{n}=A+B, and cleanup removes all work symbols. The original mm columns persist, and marker extension reaches pnp_{n}, ensuring at least n+1n+1 digits. Every additional carry extension contributes a digit required by the current numerical value. Partial sums never decrease, so the final width equals LL. ∎

Lemma H.6 (Protocol Coverage).

Every execution of ℰ\mathcal{E} from a valid input follows this protocol, starting at phase 00 and ending at phase 2626.

Proof.

The nonempty first operand establishes phases 00–33. Lemma H.4 places a digit immediately after a zero extension in phase 44, establishing phase 55. The right scan meets the separator before any blank. To the separator’s right, a first blank means the next left step reads the separator (phase 2222); after any digit, that step reads a digit (phase 99). Equation (12) guarantees two initial blank readings while transporting either bit. The cell above the marker contains a digit. A carry ends strictly left of the marker, so the first return cell contains a blank. A noncarry addition returns directly to the marker. Erasing and shifting the marker reaches a blank. Finally, cleanup starts below the separator on a blank, reaches the marker and then a digit. These facts justify every branch of the table. Induction over the steps and rounds proves coverage; Lemma H.5 supplies the final phase. ∎

Lemma H.8 (Copy Staircase).

Before product formation, the expert constructs exactly nn occupied rows. For 0≤i<n0\leq i<n, row ii contains

Row 00 contains the input. On row ii, the expert scans to the first blank, steps left to bib_{i}, then steps left again. A digit at this position implies at least two remaining right-operand bits. The expert copies every symbol except bib_{i} one row down and one column left, proceeding from right to left. Every destination contains a blank before writing; the source word remains unchanged.

The first descent reaches a blank on the new row. Each later descent reaches the copied right neighbor: a digit, except directly below the last digit of aa, where the copied separator xx occupies the lower cell. The cell below the source separator contains a digit. After copying the first digit of aa, the expert reads the blank immediately to the left and descends to the first digit of the new row.

The new row satisfies (15) for i+1i+1, with one fewer right-operand bit. When one right-operand bit remains, the second left step reads xx and starts product formation. Thus n−1n-1 copies produce exactly nn occupied rows. ∎

Lemma H.9 (Aligned Partial Products).

For bi=0b_{i}=0, the expert writes zeros; for bi=1b_{i}=1, the expert preserves the digits of aa. Both branches write one additional 00 on the left blank. Lemma H.11 (Carry Confinement).

During an upper-digit update with incoming carry 11, the lower cell contains an original binary digit. If the carry outlives the upper word, the next lower cell contains the original leading 00.

Proof.

A blank gap lies to the right of the original lower product. The first column has carry zero, and u+0+0≤1u+0+0\leq 1, so no carry originates in the gap. Lemma H.22 (Boundary Restrictions).

A carry-one update beneath an upper digit reads an original lower digit. A blank lower update guarantees another upper digit on the next left step. A carry beyond the upper word reads a lower digit in {0,…,8}\{0,\ldots,8\} and clears.

Proof.

The blank gap lies strictly to the right of the original lower word. The first update has carry zero, and u+0≤9u+0\leq 9, so no carry originates inside this gap. Carry one can first arise only inside the lower digit block; further leftward updates stay inside that block until the leading digit.

A blank lower cell has column z≥m−k−1z\geq m-k-1. The next upper column satisfies z−1≥m−k−2≥−k−1z-1\geq m-k-2\geq-k-1, using m≥1m\geq 1, and therefore still contains a digit. Finally, the lower leading digit lies one column left of the upper word. Lemma H.20 bounds this untouched digit by 88; adding 11 clears any final carry without extending the fixed-width support. ∎

Lemma H.23 (Protocol Coverage).

Every expert execution in the stated domain follows the protocol in Section H.7 from phase 00 to phase 206206.

Proof.

The following geometric and arithmetic conditions justify every read restriction.

Copying. The initial scan and every restart encounter a nonempty left operand, then xx, then a nonempty right operand before the right blank. The second left step reads a factor digit or xx. Lemma H.19 distinguishes the first descent (blank), ordinary descents (digits), and the descent directly above the copied operator (xx). Every destination contains a blank. After the first copied symbol, the next source symbol contains a digit or xx; no left blank can occur yet. After copying xx, the next source symbol contains the last digit of aa. The ordinary copy loop eventually reaches the left blank and restarts.

Products. The bottom row contains one factor digit; erasing that digit immediately exposes xx. Every higher row contains at least two factor digits; erasing the selected factor therefore exposes another digit before xx. After erasing xx, the first product update reads a digit because m≥1m\geq 1. Later updates read digits followed by the left blank. Equation (22) determines the next carry phase and preserves the carry bound. The completed product scan reads digits followed by a blank. Lemma H.20 places the head on an upper digit followed by xx and a nonempty factor prefix, or on a blank above row 00.

Alignment and Summation. Summation starts on the right blank of row 00. The initial left scan crosses a nonempty product. Inspection below reads a fresh leading digit from {0,…,8}\{0,\ldots,8\} or a blank below the last row. After a leading digit, at least one lower digit remains because m≥1m\geq 1. Lemma H.21 places the first upper alignment step on a digit; further alignment steps read digits until the right blank. The first upper units digit has carry zero and a blank lower cell.

After every lower update, the upper return cell contains the erased blank. A blank lower update leads to a nonblank upper read by Lemma H.22. An update inside the lower digit block leads to an upper digit or the left blank. Carry-one digit updates remain inside the lower digit block. At the end of the upper word, carry zero preserves the untouched lower leading digit, while carry one increments that digit and clears. Both paths reach the blank immediately left of the merged word. The final stop reads a blank.

These conditions give exactly the permitted branches used by the expert. Induction over individual moves, copied rows, and merged rows establishes coverage. The finite-pass arguments in Lemma H.19–Lemma H.21 give termination at phase 206206. ∎

Rune Semantics. Each of X,Y,ZX,Y,Z has one position and a hidden symbol. Writing a rune first restores the hidden symbol at the old rune position, then installs the rune over the symbol at the new position. Rewriting a rune in place preserves the hidden symbol. Writing an ordinary symbol at a rune removes that rune. A motion XX, YY or ZZ jumps to the corresponding rune after the write. Ordinary motions move one cell; SS stops without moving.

The logical program means the program with every rune replaced by the corresponding hidden symbol. Correctness depends on preserving this logical program, not on treating a rune as a destructive overwrite.

Endpoint and Prefix Invariant
Lemma H.25 (Endpoint and Prefix Invariant).

At the start of every simulated step, the expert occupies state 00 at the simulated tape head. Rune XX occupies column 11 on the first or last row of the current simulated state’s three-row block. After matching jj successor trits, XX occupies column 1+j1+j on a row with the correct length-jj successor prefix. The row index remains congruent to 00 or 22 modulo 33. The logical program remains unchanged.

Proof.

Initially XX occupies the first row of state 00. Assume the invariant at the start of a simulated step. The expert reads the tape symbol, installs ZZ, jumps to XX, and steps left. The symbol search selects the matching row within the current state’s three-row block. The following right scan crosses column 11 and the source code to the first delimiter, leaving XX in place.

For successor trit tt, the expert places YY on the trit, jumps to XX, and steps right to the next source-code column. All rows sharing the matched prefix form one interval. Within that interval, next-trit values increase monotonically down the table. The successor state exists, so a nonempty subinterval contains next trit tt. Moving down on a smaller trit, or up on a larger trit, reaches tt before leaving the matched-prefix interval.

An immediate match preserves the endpoint. A downward search enters the target subinterval at the first row, with read symbol λ\lambda; an upward search enters at the last row, with read symbol 11. Both rows occupy endpoints of three-row state blocks. Writing XX advances the matched prefix by one trit. Jumping to YY resumes instruction decoding.

After all κ\kappa trits, XX occupies a row in the successor state’s block. The second delimiter triggers a leftward rewind of XX to column 11 on the same row. The expert then applies the prescribed write and motion at ZZ. Rune relocation restores every covered program symbol, preserving the logical program. Each nonstopping motion establishes the next simulated step. ∎

Lemma H.26 (No Missing Middle Trit).

Within a fixed source-code prefix block, a vertical search cannot pass directly between an LL region and an SS region. A nonempty RR region separates the two regions.

Proof.

The state numbers fill the contiguous interval 0,…,N−10,\ldots,N-1, with a common encoding width. A prefix block contains a possibly truncated interval of consecutive integers. A block containing next-trit values LL and SS also contains every state in the intervening RR subinterval. Each state contributes all three read-symbol rows. ∎

Corollary H.27 (Faithful Expert Simulation).

Each simulated TM transition takes finitely many controller steps and performs the write and motion prescribed by δ\delta. The expert halts exactly when the simulated TM issues SS.

Proof.

Lemma H.25 selects the correct instruction and successor. Every scan stays within a finite program interval, and every trit search reaches a nonempty target interval. The final two instruction fields supply the prescribed write and motion at ZZ. Only a simulated SS triggers a stopping transition. ∎

Proof of Theorem H.24.

The endpoint and prefix invariant keeps every program search inside the correct code-prefix interval. The no-missing-middle-trit lemma justifies the refined search branches. Both protocols therefore cover every finite expert execution prefix on the respective domains. The metric relation satisfies 160160 local identities, and the annealing relation satisfies 162162. Equal writes and motions preserve visible cells and hidden rune symbols simultaneously. The prefix form of Lemma H.2 gives equality of complete finite PTOs and of every finite prefix for nonhalting computations. Faithful expert simulation identifies the common execution with the encoded Turing machine. ∎

Why the Metric Theorem Excludes Empty Input.

The metric controller lacks an initial blank transition. Consider a one-state machine with δ⁡(0,s)=(0,s,S)\delta(0,s)=(0,s,S) for every s∈Γs\in\Gamma and empty tape input. The expert starts with (λ,Z,X)(\lambda,Z,X), whereas the metric controller cannot take the first step. Hence extending the metric theorem to empty input would give a false claim. Later blank readings remain covered. The annealed controller handles the initial blank and needs no such restriction.

Appendix I Short-Input Agreement Does Not Identify an Algorithm

Small training datasets do not force the expert arithmetic rule, even within compact controller classes. We construct two counterexamples using the same alphabets, grid, initial placement, and action vocabulary as the binary experts. Both controllers reproduce every expert PTO within the training-length bounds, including all write and motion decisions. Both nevertheless stop prematurely on longer inputs. Thus the ambiguity persists even with exhaustive supervision over the short-input domain.

Throughout this section, a,b∈{0,1}+a,b\in{\{0,1\}}^{+} denote nonempty binary operand words, with leading zeros permitted. The input a+ba+b or a​𝚡​ba\mathtt{x}b occupies row zero from column zero; the head starts at the first left-operand digit and every other cell starts blank. Each table entry gives the next state, written symbol, and motion. Motion SS writes once and stops; the stopping-state loops specify a total transition map but add no further PTO steps. All state counts include the stopping state.

I.1 A Fourteen-State Spurious Addition Controller

The binary-addition expert uses eleven states, including the stopping state. Replace the initial scanning state by a counter with states 0,11,12,130,11,12,13, representing zero, one, two, and three scanned left-operand digits. The resulting controller contains fourteen states.

Proposition I.1 (Short-Input Agreement without Exact Addition).

The controller in Table 22 produces the expert PTO on every input a+ba+b with 1≤|a|≤31\leq|a|\leq 3 and b∈{0,1}+b\in{\{0,1\}}^{+}, including leading zeros. For every |a|≥4|a|\geq 4 and b∈{0,1}+b\in{\{0,1\}}^{+}, execution stops on the fourth left-operand digit and leaves the input unchanged.

Proof.

Before reaching the separator, the expert remains in state 00 and writes each read digit unchanged while moving right. The counter states produce exactly these writes and motions for the first three digits. On reading ++, every counter state enters expert state 11 with the same write and left move. No expert transition from states 1,…,101,\ldots,10 returns to state 00. Consequently, the controllers have identical states, grids, and heads after the separator transition and follow the same remaining execution, including the stopping action. If a fourth left-operand digit occurs, state 1313 instead writes the digit unchanged and stops, whereas the expert moves right. The unchanged input still contains ++ and therefore fails the output contract. ∎

For example, 1111+11111+1 triggers the discrepancy at step four: the expert emits (1,𝖱)(1,\mathsf{R}), while the spurious controller emits (1,𝖲)(1,\mathsf{S}). The expert eventually leaves 1000010000 on the grid. Thus even all 142=19614^{2}=196 operand pairs with lengths at most three cannot distinguish these controllers through PTO supervision.

I.2 A Thirty-Eight-State Spurious Multiplication Controller

Let T×T_{\times} denote the 32-state binary-multiplication expert. Define T~×\widetilde{T}_{\times} by retaining all expert transitions and adding six states 32,…,3732,\ldots,37 for the initial scan of the left operand. State 32+j32+j records jj digits already scanned. The initial state becomes 3232; the halt state remains 3131. The added states preserve each scanned symbol and move right, except that reading a sixth digit triggers an immediate stop. Reading the separator 𝚡\mathtt{x} enters expert state 00 with the expert’s write and motion.

Proposition I.2.

For every a∈{0,1}ma\in{\{0,1\}}^{m} with 1≤m≤51\leq m\leq 5 and every nonempty binary word bb, the complete PTOs of T~×\widetilde{T}_{\times} and T×T_{\times} on a​𝚡​ba\mathtt{x}b agree. For every left operand of at least six digits and every nonempty right operand, the spurious controller stops after six actions and leaves the input expression unchanged.

Proof.

For the first m≤5m\leq 5 digit readings, both controllers preserve the read symbol and move right. The expert remains in state 00, while the spurious controller reaches state 32+m32+m. On the separator, both controllers write 𝚡\mathtt{x}, move right, and enter state 00. The grid, head, and control state then coincide, and all remaining transitions agree. For m≥6m\geq 6, the first five actions agree, but state 3737 stops on the sixth digit while the expert moves right. Every preceding action preserves the input, so the final grid still contains the separator and both operands, violating the arithmetic output specification. ∎

For example, 111111​𝚡​1111111\mathtt{x}1 requires the product 111111111111 (decimal 6363), allowing leading-zero padding. The spurious controller instead leaves 111111​𝚡​1111111\mathtt{x}1 on the grid and halts at the sixth digit. Exhaustive enumeration of all 622=384462^{2}=3844 pairs with operand lengths from one through five confirms complete PTO agreement; the argument above additionally covers arbitrary right-operand lengths.

I.3 Capacity Does Not Exclude the Counterexamples

The constructions add only three states to the eleven-state addition expert and six states to the thirty-two-state multiplication expert. Every training subset within the stated length bounds supplies identical PTO targets for the expert and the corresponding spurious controller.

Theorem 2.5 represents the two controllers using ordinary DFST dimensions 14 and 38. For Softmax DFSTs with finite logits in exact real arithmetic, dimensions 15 and 39 suffice for exact argmax behavior. These bounds provide sufficient capacities, without asserting minimality. Padding the discrete controllers with unreachable states extends the construction to every larger dimension. In particular, the addition sweeps at dimensions 22 and 33 and the multiplication sweeps at dimensions 64 and 96 can express the counterexamples.

Action agreement and fitting the one-hot training targets require separate statements. The exact-real softmax construction in Appendix B guarantees the correct argmax actions, but need not produce one-hot readouts. For any PTO dataset within the stated training-length bounds, softmax logits approaching the deterministic vertices instead drive the MSE arbitrarily close to zero: finite-horizon recurrence and readout maps depend continuously on the effective parameters. Under rounded arithmetic that saturates softmax at vertices and preserves vertex operations, the one-hot realization gives exactly zero training MSE. One explicit choice assigns logit 00 to each selected transition, output, and initial-state coordinate, and −128-128 to every other coordinate under correctly rounded binary32 exponentiation.

The wider sweeps exclude insufficient capacity as the explanation for avoiding these two spurious rules (Tables 24 and 9). The experiments support a useful implicit bias of parametrization, initialization, and gradient-based optimization toward length-independent behavior. However, no claim identifies the failed runs with the constructed counterexamples, and the results do not establish that gradient descent always selects the simplest controller. Extracted state counts alone need not capture the relevant notion of simplicity.

I.4 A Simple Model for Studying Algorithmic Learning

The ordinary DFST uses three input-indexed tensors and an initial-state vector. Each recurrence and readout consists of a matrix-vector product, without nonlinear activations. This stepwise multilinearity offers a transparent starting point for analyzing which solutions gradient-based optimization favors. Repeated use of shared transition parameters across a trajectory still produces a nonconvex learning problem; neither the complete trajectory map nor the MSE objective generally remains multilinear in the shared parameters. The softmax parametrization adds another nonlinearity through the logits.

NeurIPS Paper Checklist

  1. 1.

    Claims

  2. Question: Do the main claims made in the abstract and introduction accurately reflect the paper’s contributions and scope?

  3. Answer: [Yes]

  4. Justification: In the abstract and introduction, we claim that we introduce a simple learning framework capable of achieving extreme length generalization and exact learning on arithmetic and universal simulation tasks. We substantiate these claims with experimental results and mathematical proofs.

  5. Guidelines:

    • •

      The answer [N/A] means that the abstract and introduction do not include the claims made in the paper.

    • •

      The abstract and/or introduction should clearly state the claims made, including the contributions made in the paper and important assumptions and limitations. A [No] or [N/A] answer to this question will not be perceived well by the reviewers.

    • •

      The claims made should match theoretical and experimental results, and reflect how much the results can be expected to generalize to other settings.

    • •

      It is fine to include aspirational goals as motivation as long as it is clear that these goals are not attained by the paper.

  6. 2.

    Limitations

  7. Question: Does the paper discuss the limitations of the work performed by the authors?

  8. Answer: [Yes]

  9. Justification: We provide evidence of hyperparameter configurations where our differentiable controllers cannot achieve extreme length generalization and provably do not exactly learn the ground-truth procedure.

  10. Guidelines:

    • •

      The answer [N/A] means that the paper has no limitation while the answer [No] means that the paper has limitations, but those are not discussed in the paper.

    • •

      The authors are encouraged to create a separate “Limitations” section in their paper.

    • •

      The paper should point out any strong assumptions and how robust the results are to violations of these assumptions (e.g., independence assumptions, noiseless settings, model well-specification, asymptotic approximations only holding locally). The authors should reflect on how these assumptions might be violated in practice and what the implications would be.

    • •

      The authors should reflect on the scope of the claims made, e.g., if the approach was only tested on a few datasets or with a few runs. In general, empirical results often depend on implicit assumptions, which should be articulated.

    • •

      The authors should reflect on the factors that influence the performance of the approach. For example, a facial recognition algorithm may perform poorly when image resolution is low or images are taken in low lighting. Or a speech-to-text system might not be used reliably to provide closed captions for online lectures because it fails to handle technical jargon.

    • •

      The authors should discuss the computational efficiency of the proposed algorithms and how they scale with dataset size.

    • •

      If applicable, the authors should discuss possible limitations of their approach to address problems of privacy and fairness.

    • •

      While the authors might fear that complete honesty about limitations might be used by reviewers as grounds for rejection, a worse outcome might be that reviewers discover limitations that aren’t acknowledged in the paper. The authors should use their best judgment and recognize that individual actions in favor of transparency play an important role in developing norms that preserve the integrity of the community. Reviewers will be specifically instructed to not penalize honesty concerning limitations.

  11. 3.

    Theory assumptions and proofs

  12. Question: For each theoretical result, does the paper provide the full set of assumptions and a complete (and correct) proof?

  13. Answer: [Yes]

  14. Justification: We provide the full set of empirically falsifiable assumptions for our theorems. All theorems are carefully proved in the appendix sections.

  15. Guidelines:

    • •

      The answer [N/A] means that the paper does not include theoretical results.

    • •

      All the theorems, formulas, and proofs in the paper should be numbered and cross-referenced.

    • •

      All assumptions should be clearly stated or referenced in the statement of any theorems.

    • •

      The proofs can either appear in the main paper or the supplemental material, but if they appear in the supplemental material, the authors are encouraged to provide a short proof sketch to provide intuition.

    • •

      Inversely, any informal proof provided in the core of the paper should be complemented by formal proofs provided in appendix or supplemental material.

    • •

      Theorems and Lemmas that the proof relies upon should be properly referenced.

  16. 4.

    Experimental result reproducibility

  17. Question: Does the paper fully disclose all the information needed to reproduce the main experimental results of the paper to the extent that it affects the main claims and/or conclusions of the paper (regardless of whether the code and data are provided or not)?

  18. Answer: [Yes]

  19. Justification: In our appendix section about implementation details, we provide full details on our training procedure. Furthermore, we make our code publicly available (alongside the weights of the runs discussed in the paper) so that other researchers can experiment with and visualize learning from Turing-machine computation.

  20. Guidelines:

    • •

      The answer [N/A] means that the paper does not include experiments.

    • •

      If the paper includes experiments, a [No] answer to this question will not be perceived well by the reviewers: Making the paper reproducible is important, regardless of whether the code and data are provided or not.

    • •

      If the contribution is a dataset and/or model, the authors should describe the steps taken to make their results reproducible or verifiable.

    • •

      Depending on the contribution, reproducibility can be accomplished in various ways. For example, if the contribution is a novel architecture, describing the architecture fully might suffice, or if the contribution is a specific model and empirical evaluation, it may be necessary to either make it possible for others to replicate the model with the same dataset, or provide access to the model. In general. releasing code and data is often one good way to accomplish this, but reproducibility can also be provided via detailed instructions for how to replicate the results, access to a hosted model (e.g., in the case of a large language model), releasing of a model checkpoint, or other means that are appropriate to the research performed.

    • •

      While NeurIPS does not require releasing code, the conference does require all submissions to provide some reasonable avenue for reproducibility, which may depend on the nature of the contribution. For example

      1. (a)

        If the contribution is primarily a new algorithm, the paper should make it clear how to reproduce that algorithm.

      2. (b)

        If the contribution is primarily a new model architecture, the paper should describe the architecture clearly and fully.

      3. (c)

        If the contribution is a new model (e.g., a large language model), then there should either be a way to access this model for reproducing the results or a way to reproduce the model (e.g., with an open-source dataset or instructions for how to construct the dataset).

      4. (d)

        We recognize that reproducibility may be tricky in some cases, in which case authors are welcome to describe the particular way they provide for reproducibility. In the case of closed-source models, it may be that access to the model is limited in some way (e.g., to registered users), but it should be possible for other researchers to have some path to reproducing or verifying the results.

  21. 5.

    Open access to data and code

  22. Question: Does the paper provide open access to the data and code, with sufficient instructions to faithfully reproduce the main experimental results, as described in supplemental material?

  23. Answer: [Yes]

  24. Justification: We provide a well documented codebase with sufficient instructions.

  25. Guidelines:

    • •

      The answer [N/A] means that paper does not include experiments requiring code.

    • •

      Please see the NeurIPS code and data submission guidelines (https://neurips.cc/public/guides/CodeSubmissionPolicy) for more details.

    • •

      While we encourage the release of code and data, we understand that this might not be possible, so [No] is an acceptable answer. Papers cannot be rejected simply for not including code, unless this is central to the contribution (e.g., for a new open-source benchmark).

    • •

      The instructions should contain the exact command and environment needed to run to reproduce the results. See the NeurIPS code and data submission guidelines (https://neurips.cc/public/guides/CodeSubmissionPolicy) for more details.

    • •

      The authors should provide instructions on data access and preparation, including how to access the raw data, preprocessed data, intermediate data, and generated data, etc.

    • •

      The authors should provide scripts to reproduce all experimental results for the new proposed method and baselines. If only a subset of experiments are reproducible, they should state which ones are omitted from the script and why.

    • •

      At submission time, to preserve anonymity, the authors should release anonymized versions (if applicable).

    • •

      Providing as much information as possible in supplemental material (appended to the paper) is recommended, but including URLs to data and code is permitted.

  26. 6.

    Experimental setting/details

  27. Question: Does the paper specify all the training and test details (e.g., data splits, hyperparameters, how they were chosen, type of optimizer) necessary to understand the results?

  28. Answer: [Yes]

  29. Justification: We completely specify all details in the appendix section about implementations. We also provide the code, hyperparameter configurations, and trained final weights in our GitHub repository.

  30. Guidelines:

    • •

      The answer [N/A] means that the paper does not include experiments.

    • •

      The experimental setting should be presented in the core of the paper to a level of detail that is necessary to appreciate the results and make sense of them.

    • •

      The full details can be provided either with the code, in appendix, or as supplemental material.

  31. 7.

    Experiment statistical significance

  32. Question: Does the paper report error bars suitably and correctly defined or other appropriate information about the statistical significance of the experiments?

  33. Answer: [Yes]

  34. Justification: Our DSFT models are deterministically initialized so the only source of randomness comes from the dataset generation. We achieve our length-generalization results across all tasks on many different random seeds (details in the appendix).

  35. Guidelines:

    • •

      The answer [N/A] means that the paper does not include experiments.

    • •

      The authors should answer [Yes] if the results are accompanied by error bars, confidence intervals, or statistical significance tests, at least for the experiments that support the main claims of the paper.

    • •

      The factors of variability that the error bars are capturing should be clearly stated (for example, train/test split, initialization, random drawing of some parameter, or overall run with given experimental conditions).

    • •

      The method for calculating the error bars should be explained (closed form formula, call to a library function, bootstrap, etc.)

    • •

      The assumptions made should be given (e.g., Normally distributed errors).

    • •

      It should be clear whether the error bar is the standard deviation or the standard error of the mean.

    • •

      It is OK to report 1-sigma error bars, but one should state it. The authors should preferably report a 2-sigma error bar than state that they have a 96% CI, if the hypothesis of Normality of errors is not verified.

    • •

      For asymmetric distributions, the authors should be careful not to show in tables or figures symmetric error bars that would yield results that are out of range (e.g., negative error rates).

    • •

      If error bars are reported in tables or plots, the authors should explain in the text how they were calculated and reference the corresponding figures or tables in the text.

  36. 8.

    Experiments compute resources

  37. Question: For each experiment, does the paper provide sufficient information on the computer resources (type of compute workers, memory, time of execution) needed to reproduce the experiments?

  38. Answer: [Yes]

  39. Justification: As we mention in the appendix, we trained on single NVIDIA A100-SXM4-40GB and Tesla V100-SXM2-32GB GPUs.

  40. Guidelines:

    • •

      The answer [N/A] means that the paper does not include experiments.

    • •

      The paper should indicate the type of compute workers CPU or GPU, internal cluster, or cloud provider, including relevant memory and storage.

    • •

      The paper should provide the amount of compute required for each of the individual experimental runs as well as estimate the total compute.

    • •

      The paper should disclose whether the full research project required more compute than the experiments reported in the paper (e.g., preliminary or failed experiments that didn’t make it into the paper).

  41. 9.

    Code of ethics

  42. Question: Does the research conducted in the paper conform, in every respect, with the NeurIPS Code of Ethics https://neurips.cc/public/EthicsGuidelines?

  43. Answer: [Yes]

  44. Justification: We carefully reviewed the ethics guidelines and confirm that our research respects them.

  45. Guidelines:

    • •

      The answer [N/A] means that the authors have not reviewed the NeurIPS Code of Ethics.

    • •

      If the authors answer [No] , they should explain the special circumstances that require a deviation from the Code of Ethics.

    • •

      The authors should make sure to preserve anonymity (e.g., if there is a special consideration due to laws or regulations in their jurisdiction).

  46. 10.

    Broader impacts

  47. Question: Does the paper discuss both potential positive societal impacts and negative societal impacts of the work performed?

  48. Answer: [N/A]

  49. Justification: This paper presents work whose goal is to advance the field of machine learning. There are many potential societal consequences of our work, none of which we feel must be specifically highlighted here.

  50. Guidelines:

    • •

      The answer [N/A] means that there is no societal impact of the work performed.

    • •

      If the authors answer [N/A] or [No] , they should explain why their work has no societal impact or why the paper does not address societal impact.

    • •

      Examples of negative societal impacts include potential malicious or unintended uses (e.g., disinformation, generating fake profiles, surveillance), fairness considerations (e.g., deployment of technologies that could make decisions that unfairly impact specific groups), privacy considerations, and security considerations.

    • •

      The conference expects that many papers will be foundational research and not tied to particular applications, let alone deployments. However, if there is a direct path to any negative applications, the authors should point it out. For example, it is legitimate to point out that an improvement in the quality of generative models could be used to generate Deepfakes for disinformation. On the other hand, it is not needed to point out that a generic algorithm for optimizing neural networks could enable people to train models that generate Deepfakes faster.

    • •

      The authors should consider possible harms that could arise when the technology is being used as intended and functioning correctly, harms that could arise when the technology is being used as intended but gives incorrect results, and harms following from (intentional or unintentional) misuse of the technology.

    • •

      If there are negative societal impacts, the authors could also discuss possible mitigation strategies (e.g., gated release of models, providing defenses in addition to attacks, mechanisms for monitoring misuse, mechanisms to monitor how a system learns from feedback over time, improving the efficiency and accessibility of ML).

  51. 11.

    Safeguards

  52. Question: Does the paper describe safeguards that have been put in place for responsible release of data or models that have a high risk for misuse (e.g., pre-trained language models, image generators, or scraped datasets)?

  53. Answer: [N/A]

  54. Justification: We don’t believe our research holds such risks.

  55. Guidelines:

    • •

      The answer [N/A] means that the paper poses no such risks.

    • •

      Released models that have a high risk for misuse or dual-use should be released with necessary safeguards to allow for controlled use of the model, for example by requiring that users adhere to usage guidelines or restrictions to access the model or implementing safety filters.

    • •

      Datasets that have been scraped from the Internet could pose safety risks. The authors should describe how they avoided releasing unsafe images.

    • •

      We recognize that providing effective safeguards is challenging, and many papers do not require this, but we encourage authors to take this into account and make a best faith effort.

      For existing datasets that are re-packaged, both the original license and the license of the derived asset (if it has changed) should be provided.

    • •

      If this information is not available online, the authors are encouraged to reach out to the asset’s creators.
